title: German foundations
description: 52 German lessons in 17 units. Units 1-12 (35 lessons, CEFR A1) cover first words, introductions, polite café requests, numbers and quantities, directions, prices, days and times, family, the weather, free time, home and articles, describing things, plurals, daily routine, negation, asking questions, food and drink, possession, transport, polite requests, the past, making plans, months and dates, telling the time, the market, health and the body, the pharmacy, emergencies, and invitations. Units 13-17 (17 lessons, CEFR A2) add talking about the past (Perfekt with haben and sein, Präteritum of modals, weekend stories), the future (Futur I for plans and guesses, resolutions), wishes and politeness (würde, polite requests, unreal wishes), connecting sentences (relative clauses, comparatives, superlatives, wo vs wohin), and work life (passive with werden, job vocabulary, a job-interview mission). Lesson types mix discovery, conversation, story, mission, construction, and recall practice. Editorial review is AI-assisted and developer-led against the project rubric; native-speaker review is pending for the whole pack.

concepts.title: First words and greetings
concepts.explanation: German greetings follow the hour rather than the person: Guten Morgen, Guten Tag, Guten Abend. Hallo ignores the clock and is what you will actually hear most. The habit worth starting on day one is that every German noun takes a capital letter wherever it sits in a sentence, so Kaffee and Nation look like names even in the middle of a line.
concepts.commonError: Say hallo the moment you arrive — Germans notice silence more than accent. Save tschüss (goodbye) for leaving.

concepts.title: Introducing yourself
concepts.explanation: German introduces you with heißen, 'to be called': Ich heiße Anna. The verb changes with the person — ich heiße, du heißt — and keeps its ß. A question simply moves the verb in front of the person: Wie heißt du? Ich bin Anna is the alternative, built on plain 'to be'.
concepts.commonError: Use heiße with ich and heißt with du. Keep the capital letter at the beginning of a sentence.

concepts.title: Polite café requests
concepts.explanation: German requests a drink with Ich möchte, 'I would like'. Once the drink is what is being asked for, the article turns into einen: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. Kaffee and Tee are masculine nouns and keep their capitals.

examples.meaning: I would like a coffee, please.
I would like a tea, please.

concepts.commonError: Use einen in these requests, not ein. German nouns keep their capitals: Kaffee and Tee.

concepts.title: Numbers and quantities
concepts.explanation: German numbers are worth having as short runs before you calculate with them, and they take a turn at twenty: einundzwanzig is 'one-and-twenty', with the smaller number spoken first and welded to the ten by und. Learn one through ten first, then ask a price with Was kostet?. Expect the article in front of the noun to change with the job it does, and keep the noun's capital wherever it sits.

examples.meaning: How much does a coffee cost?

concepts.commonError: Use ein with one masculine Apfel and zwei with plural Äpfel. German nouns are capitalized.

concepts.title: Asking the way
concepts.explanation: German builds the names of its places out of smaller nouns stuck together, and that is why the article is worth noticing: der Bahnhof is Bahn plus Hof, a 'rail-yard', and it stays a capitalised der wherever it sits. To ask about it, German puts the verb straight after the question word, Wo ist der Bahnhof?, because the question word takes the first slot and the verb must take the second. Directions then arrive as chunks worth learning whole: geradeaus, links, rechts, with dann linking one step to the next.

examples.meaning: Excuse me, where is the toilet?

concepts.commonError: Wo asks where. Wer asks who, and was asks what. Mixing up wo and wer sends you to the wrong question entirely.

concepts.title: Prices and paying
concepts.explanation: German writes a price with a comma where English writes a point, and hangs the Euro sign after the number: 3,50 € is three euros fifty. The price question is verb-second — Was kostet das? puts the question word first and the verb straight behind it. Günstig praises the value; billig also means cheap but it hints at shoddy goods, so the two are not interchangeable in a shop.

examples.meaning: How much does the coffee cost?

concepts.commonError: Nicht goes before the adjective it negates: nicht teuer. Putting it after changes the sentence into something German does not say.

concepts.title: Days and times
concepts.explanation: The German week is named, not numbered: Sonntag and Montag for the sun and the moon, Dienstag and Donnerstag and Freitag for old gods, and Mittwoch, the odd one out, which just marks the middle. Weekdays are masculine, so am Montag. Say morgen and you mean tomorrow; say der Morgen and you mean the morning.
concepts.commonError: Morgen means tomorrow. Der Morgen means the morning. The article is the whole difference, and the capital letter marks the noun.

concepts.title: Family and people
concepts.explanation: German sorts every noun into one of three genders and shows it in the article: der Bruder, die Schwester, die Eltern. Only the masculine nouns reveal the accusative when they are the thing you have — Ich habe einen Bruder but Ich habe eine Schwester. Eltern is plural with no singular at all, and Geschwister does the same job for brothers and sisters together: German keeps one plural word for siblings and no word for a single sibling.
concepts.commonError: Einen Bruder, not ein Bruder: the direct object takes the accusative, and only masculine nouns change.

concepts.title: Weather and seasons
concepts.explanation: German hands the weather to a small word and then says what it is doing: es regnet, es ist kalt, es schneit. That es is not the English it — it stands in for the whole situation, so it never changes, whatever the weather is doing. The sun is the exception worth noticing: it does the shining itself, as a subject with a verb of its own, so the sentence reads die Sonne scheint. And because German keeps the verb in second place, fronting the place pushes the tiny word past it: es regnet in Hamburg becomes In Hamburg regnet es.
concepts.commonError: Regnet es, not es regnet, once the place comes first: In Hamburg regnet es.

concepts.title: Free time and hobbies
concepts.explanation: English says you like doing something with a second verb; German uses one small word instead and keeps it next to the verb it belongs to. Ich lese gern is literally I read gladly, and the gern cannot drift to the front or the end — it rides directly behind the verb. Move the sentence to wir or sie and only the verb changes: Ich spiele gern Tennis becomes Wir spielen gern Tennis. Freizeit is the same trick German plays all over its vocabulary: frei plus Zeit, free plus time, written as one word.
concepts.commonError: Ich gern spiele, not Ich spiele gern: the little word sits right after the verb.

concepts.title: Home and articles
concepts.explanation: German gives every noun a gender, and the article shows it: der Tisch is masculine, die Küche is feminine, das Zimmer is neuter. The indefinite article follows the same three-way split — ein Tisch, eine Küche, ein Zimmer: ein goes with der and das, eine only with die. Learn each noun together with its article, because the gender never changes.
concepts.commonError: Eine Tisch is wrong: Tisch is masculine, so it takes ein, not eine.

concepts.title: Describing things
concepts.explanation: After ist, a German adjective never changes: das Auto ist groß, die Küche ist klein, das Zimmer ist neu — groß, klein and neu look exactly the same for every gender. Sehr works like English very and sits right before the adjective: das Auto ist sehr groß. Word order stays simple: subject, ist, then the description.
concepts.commonError: Das Auto ist große is wrong: after ist the adjective never takes an ending.

concepts.title: More than one
concepts.explanation: Every plural article is die, whatever the gender was: der Tisch becomes die Tische, das Kind becomes die Kinder. German builds plurals in a few favorite ways — add -e (Tisch → Tische), add -er, sometimes with an umlaut (Kind → Kinder), add -e plus an umlaut (Stuhl → Stühle), add -en (Frau → Frauen), or just add -s (Auto → Autos). Learn each plural with its singular; the pattern is a hint, not a rule.
concepts.commonError: Die Tischs is wrong: Tisch takes -e in the plural — die Tische — and the verb must be plural too: sind, not ist.

concepts.title: Work and daily routine
concepts.explanation: German verbs end in -en, and the ich-form drops the -n: arbeiten becomes ich arbeite, lernen becomes ich lerne. Time-of-day words like morgens, mittags and abends sit right after the verb: Ich arbeite morgens. They answer when, and German puts the when directly behind the action.
concepts.commonError: Ich arbeiten morgens is wrong: with ich the verb loses its -n — ich arbeite.

concepts.title: Saying no
concepts.explanation: German has two ways to say no. Kein negates a noun and behaves like ein — kein Tisch, keine Küche, kein Zimmer: it matches the noun’s gender. Nicht negates everything else — verbs and adjectives: Ich arbeite nicht, das Zimmer ist nicht groß. If there is a noun to negate, reach for kein; otherwise reach for nicht.
concepts.commonError: Ich habe nicht Auto is wrong: a noun needs kein — Ich habe kein Auto.

concepts.title: Asking questions
concepts.explanation: German question words all start with w: wer asks who, was asks what, wo asks where, wann asks when, wie asks how. The question word takes first position and the verb comes second: Wo arbeitest du? A yes-no question skips the question word and puts the verb first: Arbeitest du? The verb still matches its subject — arbeitest for du.
concepts.commonError: Wo du arbeitest? is wrong: the verb must come second — Wo arbeitest du?

concepts.title: Food and drink
concepts.explanation: Essen and trinken are strong verbs: the ich-form changes its vowel — ich esse, ich trinke. Mögen is softer: ich mag, and it takes a noun directly — Ich mag Käse. German eats and drinks with the verb in second position, and gern still sits behind it: Ich esse gern Brot.
concepts.commonError: Ich essen Brot is wrong: with ich the verb is esse — Ich esse Brot.

concepts.title: Mine and yours
concepts.explanation: German possessives copy the noun’s gender like ein does: mein Bruder, meine Schwester, mein Kind. Dein means your, sein means his, ihr means her — and each of them changes the same way: dein Bruder, deine Schwester. In the nominative you only need to watch the feminine -e.
concepts.commonError: Das ist mein Schwester is wrong: Schwester is feminine, so the possessive needs -e — meine Schwester.

concepts.title: Getting around
concepts.explanation: German splits going in two: gehen is on foot — Ich gehe zu Fuß — while fahren covers everything with wheels: Ich fahre mit dem Bus. Fliegen is for planes. Mit always takes the dative, so it is mit dem Bus and mit dem Zug, never mit den. For cities, nach does the job with no article: nach Berlin.
concepts.commonError: Ich gehe mit dem Bus is wrong: gehen is on foot — by bus is Ich fahre mit dem Bus.

concepts.title: Polite requests
concepts.explanation: Können means can and möchten means would like — both are modal verbs, and modals send the main verb to the very end: Ich kann Deutsch sprechen, Ich möchte einen Kaffee trinken. Möchten is the polite engine of every café order: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. The modal itself conjugates normally: ich kann, du kannst.
concepts.commonError: Ich kann sprechen Deutsch is wrong: the modal pushes sprechen to the end — Ich kann Deutsch sprechen.

concepts.title: Yesterday: a first look at the past
concepts.explanation: Spoken German builds the past with haben plus a participle at the end: Ich habe gelernt, ich habe gegessen. Most participles wear ge- at the front and -t at the back: machen → gemacht, lernen → gelernt. A few strong verbs change their vowel: essen → gegessen, trinken → getrunken. Haben conjugates normally; the participle never moves from the end.
concepts.commonError: Ich habe lernen is wrong: the past needs the participle — Ich habe gelernt.

concepts.title: Making plans
concepts.explanation: German rarely needs a future tense: the present plus a time word does the job. Morgen arbeite ich, nächste Woche fliege ich — the time word takes first position and the verb stays second, so the subject slides behind it. Bald, später and nächste Woche are all you need to plan ahead.
concepts.commonError: Morgen ich arbeite is wrong: with a time word first, the verb stays second — Morgen arbeite ich.

concepts.title: Months, seasons and dates
concepts.explanation: German months are masculine: der Januar, der Mai, der Dezember. Dates use am with the number and a dot: am 3. Mai — literally ‘on the 3rd of May’. In a month is im: im Mai, im Winter. The four seasons are der Frühling, der Sommer, der Herbst, der Winter.
concepts.commonError: An 3. Mai is wrong: dates take am — am 3. Mai.

concepts.title: Telling the time
concepts.explanation: Wie spät ist es? asks the time, and the answer starts with Es ist. Halb drei is the famous trap: it means half past TWO — German counts the half toward the coming hour. Viertel nach drei is quarter past three, viertel vor drei is quarter to three. Die Uhr is the clock, and … Uhr marks the hour: drei Uhr.
concepts.commonError: Halb drei is not half past three — German counts toward the coming hour, so halb drei is 2:30.

concepts.title: At the market
concepts.explanation: At the market you buy amounts: ein Kilo Äpfel, eine Flasche Wasser, ein Stück Käse. The amount word takes the gender — ein Kilo, eine Flasche, ein Stück — and the food follows without an article. Ich nehme… (I’ll take…) is the market’s favorite sentence, and gern says you like what you chose: Ich nehme gern Käse.

examples.meaning: I’ll take a kilo of apples.
I’ll take a bottle of water.

concepts.commonError: Ein Flasche Wasser is wrong: Flasche is feminine — eine Flasche Wasser.

concepts.title: Health and the body
concepts.explanation: Body parts wear their articles: der Kopf, der Arm, das Bein. Pain in German happens to you, not in you: Mir tut der Kopf weh — literally ‘to me does the head hurt’. Zum Arzt gehen is to go to the doctor, with zum packing zu plus dem.
concepts.commonError: Mein Kopf tut weh is understandable but unidiomatic: German says Mir tut der Kopf weh.

concepts.title: At the pharmacy
concepts.explanation: Brauchen means to need and takes the accusative like haben does: Ich brauche eine Tablette, ich brauche ein Medikament. Gegen means against and also takes the accusative: gegen Kopfschmerzen. Etwas is the useful vagueness of the pharmacy queue: Ich brauche etwas gegen Kopfschmerzen.

examples.meaning: I need something for a headache.

concepts.commonError: Ich brauche ein Tablette is wrong: Tablette is feminine — eine Tablette.

concepts.title: Emergencies
concepts.explanation: Hilfe! is the word that starts every emergency. The formal command puts the verb first and keeps Sie: Rufen Sie den Arzt! The du-form drops the ending: Ruf den Arzt! The emergency number is 112 — der Notruf — one number for the whole EU.
concepts.commonError: Sie rufen den Arzt! is a statement, not a command: the imperative starts with the verb — Rufen Sie den Arzt!

concepts.title: Invitations
concepts.explanation: Einladen is a separable verb: the ein jumps to the end — Ich lade dich ein. Accept with Ja, gern! and decline softly with Leider kann ich nicht. Time and place ride along as always: am Samstag, in Berlin.
concepts.commonError: Ich einlade dich is wrong: ein separates and goes last — Ich lade dich ein.

concepts.title: Perfekt with haben
concepts.explanation: The spoken past is two pieces: haben in second position + the participle at the very end. For regular verbs the participle is easy: ge- + stem + -t — spielen becomes gespielt, kochen becomes gekocht. Word order does the rest: Ich habe gestern gekocht.
concepts.commonError: Saying *Ich habe spiele is wrong — the participle needs its ge-...-t costume: Ich habe gespielt.

concepts.title: Perfekt with sein
concepts.explanation: Some verbs travel with sein instead of haben: verbs of movement and change of place — gehen, kommen, fahren, bleiben. Ich bin gegangen, not *ich habe gegangen. And the famous irregulars change their stem: kommen becomes gekommen, fahren becomes gefahren, essen becomes gegessen, sehen becomes gesehen.
concepts.commonError: Saying *Ich habe gegangen is wrong — gehen means movement, so it takes sein: Ich bin gegangen.

concepts.title: Präteritum of modals, sein, haben
concepts.explanation: In stories, German drops the two-word Perfekt and uses one word: ich war, ich hatte, ich konnte, ich musste. The modals lose their umlaut in the past — müssen becomes musste, können becomes konnte, dürfen becomes durfte, sollen becomes sollte, wollen becomes wollte, mögen becomes mochte. Sein and haben join them: war, hatte. When you narrate, reach for these.
concepts.commonError: Writing *ich müßte is wrong — the umlaut disappears in the Präteritum: ich musste.

concepts.title: Narrating with Perfekt
concepts.explanation: A story needs signposts: zuerst (first), dann (then), danach (afterwards), am Ende (at the end). Each one kicks the verb into second position: Zuerst habe ich gefrühstückt. Dann bin ich spazieren gegangen. String Perfekt sentences together with these connectors and you sound like you're really telling it, not reciting it.

examples.meaning: Then I went for a walk.

examples.target: Danach haben wir einen Film gesehen.

examples.meaning: In the end we were tired.

concepts.commonError: Writing *Zuerst ich habe is wrong — the connector counts as position one, so the verb comes next: Zuerst habe ich...

concepts.title: Futur I with werden
concepts.explanation: The future is werden + infinitive, with the infinitive waiting at the end: Ich werde reisen, du wirst kommen, er wird lernen, wir werden feiern. Werden carries the person; the main verb stays untouched at the end. One frame — Ich werde ... — opens every plan.
concepts.commonError: Writing *Ich werde reise is wrong — the main verb stays an infinitive at the end: Ich werde reisen.

concepts.title: Futur I for assumptions
concepts.explanation: Futur I isn't only the future — it's German's guessing machine. Er wird wohl krank sein doesn't mean 'he will be sick'; it means 'he's probably sick right now'. Add wohl, sicherlich or schon and the future form guesses about the present: Sie wird schon zu Hause sein. Das wird stimmen.

examples.target: Sie wird schon zu Hause sein.

examples.meaning: Where can he be, I wonder?

concepts.commonError: Don't translate wird as 'will' here: Er wird krank sein guesses about now, not the future.

concepts.title: Plans and resolutions
concepts.explanation: German has a dedicated plan-machine: Ich habe vor, ... zu ... — 'I plan to ...'. Ich habe vor, mehr Sport zu machen. Mein Vorsatz: weniger Süßigkeiten. Pair it with the future you just learned — Ich werde mehr lesen — and add time words: nächstes Jahr, ab morgen, bald.

examples.target: Ich habe vor, mehr Sport zu machen.
examples.meaning: I plan to do more sport.

concepts.commonError: After vor, the verb needs zu: Ich habe vor, *Sport machen is wrong — say Sport zu machen.

concepts.title: Konjunktiv II with würde
concepts.explanation: Würde + infinitive is German's 'would': ich würde, du würdest, er würde, wir würden, ihr würdet, sie würden — then the infinitive at the end. Ich würde gern reisen. Würdest du mir helfen? It softens wishes, requests, and daydreams alike. One frame, endless politeness.
concepts.commonError: Writing *ich würdete is wrong — würde is already the full form: ich würde, du würdest.

concepts.title: Polite requests
concepts.explanation: Polite German runs on soft questions: Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen? Würden Sie das Fenster öffnen? Wäre es möglich, später zu kommen? The recipe: modal in the würde or könnte form + bitte + infinitive at the end. Commands demand; these questions invite.

examples.target: Wäre es möglich, später zu kommen?
examples.meaning: Would it be possible to come later?

concepts.commonError: Kannst du bitte... is okay but blunt — Könntest du...? is the polite version.

concepts.title: Unreal wishes
concepts.explanation: For wishes that can't come true, German has a special sigh: Ich wünschte, ich wäre in Italien. Wenn ich nur mehr Zeit hätte! The verbs shift into the unreal: wäre (were), hätte (had), könnte (could). It's the grammar of daydreams — learn wäre, hätte and könnte and you can wish for anything.

examples.target: Ich wünschte, ich wäre in Italien.
examples.meaning: I wish I were in Italy.

examples.target: Wenn ich nur mehr Zeit hätte!
examples.meaning: If only I had more time!
If only I had studied more!

concepts.commonError: In a wish, ich takes wäre, not *würde sein: Ich wünschte, ich wäre reich.

concepts.title: Relative clauses
concepts.explanation: A relative clause glues description onto a noun: der Mann, der dort wohnt. The relative pronoun copies the noun's gender and number — der Mann goes with der, die Frau with die, das Buch with das — and the verb moves to the very end: das Buch, das ich lese. Commas mark the clause: one sentence, twice the information.

examples.target: Der Mann, der dort wohnt, ist nett.
examples.meaning: The man who lives there is nice.

examples.target: Die Frau, die ich kenne, lacht.
examples.meaning: The woman I know is laughing.

examples.target: Das Buch, das du liest, ist gut.
examples.meaning: The book you're reading is good.

examples.target: Der Film, den wir sahen, war toll.
examples.meaning: The film we saw was great.

concepts.commonError: The pronoun must match the noun: *die Mann, der is wrong — say der Mann, der. And the verb goes last in the clause.

concepts.title: The comparative
concepts.explanation: Comparing is easy: add -er and follow with als. Groß becomes größer als, schnell becomes schneller als, billig becomes billiger als. Three rebels change completely: gut becomes besser, viel becomes mehr, gern becomes lieber. Berlin ist größer als München — one ending, one word, done.

examples.target: Ich lerne lieber Deutsch als Mathe.
examples.meaning: I prefer learning German to maths.

examples.target: Das ist billiger als das Hotel.

concepts.commonError: Writing *größer wie is wrong — the comparative always pairs with als: größer als.

concepts.title: The superlative
concepts.explanation: The superlative has two outfits. Alone after the verb: am + -sten — Das ist am besten, Er läuft am schnellsten. Before a noun: der, die, das + -ste — der schnellste Zug, die schönste Stadt. Same three rebels as the comparative: gut becomes best-, viel becomes meist-, gern becomes liebst-.

examples.target: Der ICE ist der schnellste Zug.
examples.meaning: The ICE is the fastest train.
Berlin is the most interesting city.

concepts.commonError: Writing *am beste is wrong — after am comes -sten: am besten, am schnellsten.

concepts.title: Two-way prepositions
concepts.explanation: Nine prepositions change case with one question: wo? (where) takes Dativ, wohin? (where to) takes Akkusativ. Ich bin in der Küche (wo, Dativ) versus Ich gehe in die Küche (wohin, Akkusativ). Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch versus Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch. In, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen — ask wo or wohin, and the case answers itself.

examples.target: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
examples.meaning: The book is lying on the table.

examples.target: Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch.
examples.meaning: I'm putting the book on the table.

concepts.commonError: Writing *Ich gehe in der Küche mixes them: wohin needs Akkusativ — Ich gehe in die Küche.

concepts.title: Passive with werden
concepts.explanation: The passive spotlights the action, not the actor: werden + Partizip II. Das Auto wird repariert — 'the car is being repaired' (by whom? doesn't matter). Die E-Mails werden geschrieben. Don't confuse it with the future: wird gemacht means 'is being done', right now.
concepts.commonError: Writing *Die Briefe werden schreiben is active — the passive needs the participle: werden geschrieben.

concepts.title: Jobs and applications
concepts.explanation: Work talk has its own vocabulary: der Beruf (profession), die Stelle (position), sich bewerben (to apply), das Vorstellungsgespräch (job interview), das Gehalt (salary), der Lebenslauf (CV). The key sentence: Ich bewerbe mich um eine Stelle als... — 'I'm applying for a position as...'. Say it and you sound employable.

examples.target: Ich bewerbe mich um eine Stelle.

concepts.commonError: Bewerben needs mich and um: Ich bewerbe *mich um eine Stelle — don't drop the mich.

vocabulary.example: Im Urlaub bin ich viel gefahren.
In der Zukunft werde ich reisen.
Ich nehme mir vor, zu lesen.
Ich höre mit dem Naschen auf.
Kannst du mir einen Gefallen tun?
Wenn ich Zeit habe, komme ich.
Ich bewerbe mich um die Stelle.

stimuli.translation: I have a small family: one brother and one sister. My brother still lives in Hamburg, my sister has moved to Vienna. Only my parents have stayed in Berlin.

stimuli.body: Deine Mission: leave the Saturday market with two apples, one coffee to take away, and the bill paid — everything in German. The list: zwei Äpfel, einen Kaffee, die Rechnung.
The price board at the stall reads: Apfel — 1 Euro. Kaffee — 2 Euro.
Ich wohne in einer kleinen Wohnung. Das Zimmer ist klein und das Bett ist alt. Die Küche ist neu und der Tisch ist groß.
stimuli.translation: I live in a small apartment. The room is small and the bed is old. The kitchen is new and the table is big.

stimuli.body: Mein Haus ist alt, aber die Küche ist neu und sehr groß. Das Zimmer ist klein und sehr alt. Der Tisch ist groß.
stimuli.translation: My house is old, but the kitchen is new and very big. The room is small and very old. The table is big.

pairs.target: Der Tisch ist groß. Die Tische sind groß.
pairs.meaning: The table is big. The tables are big.

pairs.target: Das Kind ist klein. Die Kinder sind klein.
pairs.meaning: The child is small. The children are small.

pairs.target: Das Auto ist neu. Die Autos sind neu.
pairs.meaning: The car is new. The cars are new.

stimuli.body: Ich arbeite morgens und lerne abends. Mittags esse ich. Nachts schlafe ich.
stimuli.translation: I work in the morning and learn in the evening. At midday I eat. At night I sleep.

stimuli.body: Wer bist du? Ich bin Anna. Wo wohnst du? Ich wohne in Berlin.
stimuli.translation: Who are you? I’m Anna. Where do you live? I live in Berlin.

stimuli.body: Ich esse morgens Brot und trinke Wasser. Mittags esse ich Käse. Ich mag Äpfel sehr.
stimuli.translation: In the morning I eat bread and drink water. At midday I eat cheese. I like apples very much.

stimuli.body: Das ist mein Bruder. Das ist meine Schwester. Sein Auto ist neu, aber ihre Tasche ist klein.
stimuli.translation: That is my brother. That is my sister. His car is new, but her bag is small.

stimuli.body: Mein Plan: morgen lerne ich. Nächste Woche besuche ich meine Eltern. Bald fliege ich nach Wien.
stimuli.translation: My plan: tomorrow I learn. Next week I visit my parents. Soon I fly to Vienna.

stimuli.body: Mein Geburtstag ist am 3. Mai. Im Sommer besuche ich meine Familie. Der Winter ist kalt, aber ich mag den Winter.
stimuli.translation: My birthday is on May 3rd. In summer I visit my family. Winter is cold, but I like winter.

pairs.meaning: I’ll take a kilo of apples.
I’ll take a bottle of water.
I’ll take a piece of cheese.

stimuli.body: Mir tut der Kopf weh. Ich gehe zum Arzt. Der Arzt ist nett. Morgen bleibe ich zu Hause.
stimuli.translation: My head hurts. I’m going to the doctor. The doctor is nice. Tomorrow I’m staying home.

pairs.meaning: I need something for a headache.

stimuli.body: Ich lade dich zu meiner Party ein. Die Party ist am Samstag. Kommst du? Ja, ich komme gern!
stimuli.translation: I’m inviting you to my party. The party is on Saturday. Are you coming? Yes, I’d love to come!

stimuli.body: Ich habe einen Wunsch: ich würde gern mehr reisen. Eigentlich würde ich gern in Italien leben. Würdest du mitkommen? Das wäre toll!
stimuli.translation: I have a wish: I would like to travel more. Actually I would like to live in Italy. Would you come along? That would be great!

pairs.target: Wäre es möglich, später zu kommen?
pairs.meaning: Would it be possible to come later?

stimuli.body: Im Hotel: 'Wäre es möglich, später zu kommen?' — 'Selbstverständlich! Könnten Sie bitte einen Moment warten?' — 'Gern. Würden Sie das Fenster öffnen? Es ist warm hier.'
stimuli.translation: At the hotel: 'Would it be possible to come later?' — 'Of course! Could you please wait a moment?' — 'Gladly. Would you open the window? It's warm in here.'

pairs.target: Ich wünschte, ich wäre in Italien.
pairs.meaning: I wish I were in Italy.

pairs.target: Wenn ich nur mehr Zeit hätte!
pairs.meaning: If only I had more time!

pairs.target: Der Mann, der dort wohnt, ist nett.
pairs.meaning: The man who lives there is nice.

pairs.target: Die Frau, die ich kenne, lacht.
pairs.meaning: The woman I know is laughing.

pairs.target: Das Buch, das du liest, ist gut.
pairs.meaning: The book you're reading is good.

pairs.target: Die Wohnung, die wir mieten, ist ruhig.
pairs.meaning: The apartment we're renting is quiet.

pairs.target: Mein Auto ist schneller als deins.
pairs.meaning: My car is faster than yours.

pairs.target: Das Hostel ist billiger als das Hotel.
pairs.meaning: The hostel is cheaper than the hotel.

stimuli.body: Zwei Hotels: Das Hotel Adlon ist teurer als das Hostel. Aber das Hostel ist besser als sein Ruf! Die Zimmer sind größer als im Hotel, und das Frühstück ist billiger als in der Stadt.
stimuli.translation: Two hotels: Hotel Adlon is more expensive than the hostel. But the hostel is better than its reputation! The rooms are bigger than in the hotel, and breakfast is cheaper than in town.

pairs.target: Der ICE ist der schnellste Zug.
pairs.meaning: The ICE is the fastest train.

pairs.target: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
pairs.meaning: The book is on the table.

pairs.target: Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch.
pairs.meaning: I put the book on the table.

stimuli.body: Wir stellen das Sofa an die Wand. Der Stuhl steht neben dem Tisch. Das Bild hängt über dem Sofa. Die Lampe liegt noch auf dem Boden — wir stellen sie in die Ecke.
stimuli.translation: We're putting the sofa against the wall. The chair stands next to the table. The picture hangs above the sofa. The lamp is still lying on the floor — we're putting it in the corner.

stimuli.body: In der Fabrik wird viel gearbeitet. Die Produkte werden hier gebaut und dann verkauft. Jeden Tag werden tausend Pakete geliefert. Hier wird Deutsch gesprochen.
stimuli.translation: A lot is worked in the factory. The products are built here and then sold. Every day a thousand parcels are delivered. German is spoken here.

pairs.target: Ich bewerbe mich um eine Stelle.

stimuli.body: Stellenanzeige: Wir suchen einen Mitarbeiter. Der Beruf: Verkäufer. Das Gehalt ist gut. Bitte schicken Sie Ihren Lebenslauf. Das Vorstellungsgespräch ist nächste Woche.
stimuli.translation: Job ad: We're looking for an employee. The profession: salesperson. The salary is good. Please send your CV. The interview is next week.

pairs.meaning: I would like to work here.

pairs.target: Ich habe drei Jahre in Berlin gearbeitet.
pairs.meaning: I worked in Berlin for three years.
Thank you very much for the interview.

activities.body: It is 10 a.m. in Berlin. You stop at a café counter before catching a tram. Greet the server, ask for a coffee, and thank them when it arrives. The order uses einen Kaffee; notice that extra -n as you say the three lines below.

activities.prompt: The server pauses at the counter. Which greeting starts your order?
hints: The exchange starts with a greeting — the word you say when you arrive, not when you order or leave.
activities.feedback: Hallo opens this short exchange. Now you can ask for the coffee.

activities.prompt: Build the order: A coffee, please.
hints: Open with the object form of 'a' (Einen), then the drink Kaffee, and close with bitte.
activities.feedback: Einen Kaffee, bitte. The -n belongs to the thing you are ordering.

activities.prompt: The coffee is ready. How do you thank the server?
hints: The coffee has arrived — thank the server. The word starts like English 'thanks'.
activities.feedback: Danke is the last line of your exchange.

activities.prompt: Say the order once in your head. Then write in German: A coffee, please.
hints: You built this with the word tiles a moment ago: Einen (object form of 'a') + Kaffee + bitte.
activities.feedback: You wrote the order without the tiles.

errors.explanation: The coffee is the thing you are ordering, so the masculine article takes the object form: einen Kaffee, not ein Kaffee.
Add bitte — the polite 'please' — to complete the request: Einen Kaffee, bitte.

activities.prompt: Match the three lines you used to their meanings.
hints: Match each line to what it says in English, and let the order of your exchange guide you: greeting first, then the order, then the thanks.
activities.feedback: You can recognize the whole exchange.

activities.prompt: Write the three lines in order: Hello. / A coffee, please. / Thank you.
hints: Write the three lines in the order you used them — greeting, order, thanks — exactly the forms you matched just before.
activities.feedback: You opened the exchange, ordered, and thanked the server.

errors.explanation: The order line needs the object form: einen Kaffee, not ein Kaffee.
The exchange runs greeting → order → thanks: Hallo. Einen Kaffee, bitte. Danke.

activities.body: The everyday way to give your name is heißen, which means 'to be called', so Ich heiße Anna is literally 'I am called Anna'. The verb changes shape with the person: ich heiße, but du heißt, and the ß stays in both. A statement puts the verb second (Ich heiße Anna); to ask, German moves the verb in front of the person behind a question word — Wie heißt du? Ich bin Anna is the other introduction, and there you use plain 'to be'.

activities.prompt: German has a verb that means 'to be called'. Which of these introduces you with that verb?
hints: The verb that means 'to be called' is heißen. Pick the sentence that introduces a name with it — not the one built on 'to be' (bin) and not the question.
activities.feedback: Ich heiße Anna is literally 'I am called Anna'. Ich bin Anna also gives a name, but it uses plain 'to be', and Wie heißt du? is the question, not an introduction.

activities.prompt: You meet a neighbour. Introduce yourself as Anna with the verb that means 'to be called'.
hints: Use the verb heißen: with ich it becomes heiße, and the lesson's name to introduce is Anna.
activities.feedback: Ich heiße, not Ich bin, when the verb 'to be called' carries the name.

errors.explanation: Ich bin Anna says 'I am Anna', built on sein ('to be'). The step asks for the verb that means 'to be called': Ich heiße Anna.
Ich takes heiße; heißt is the du-form. Pair ich with heiße: Ich heiße Anna.
The introduction names you — end with the name: Ich heiße Anna.

activities.prompt: The three words are out of order. Build the sentence in which Anna is called by name using heißen.
hints: Open with Ich (capital I), then the verb heiße in second position, then the name Anna.
activities.feedback: Use heiße with ich and heißt with du. The verb sits second, and Ich keeps its capital as it opens the sentence.

activities.prompt: Your new colleague has introduced himself. Answer with the short German phrase for 'Nice to meet you'.
hints: The short reply starts with F and ends with mich — freut ('pleases') + mich ('me'): Freut mich.
activities.feedback: Freut mich is the short reply German uses straight after an introduction.

errors.explanation: That is a word-for-word translation. German answers an introduction with the short fixed phrase Freut mich.
Ich freue mich means 'I am pleased', but it is not the reply to an introduction. The fixed short phrase is Freut mich.

activities.prompt: Learn a classmate's name by asking the question in which the verb comes before the person.
hints: Start with the question word Wie, then the du-form of heißen (heißt), then du. No extra helping word is needed.
activities.feedback: German forms this question by putting heißt before du, with Wie in front — no extra helping word is needed.

errors.explanation: With du the verb is heißt; heiße goes with ich. Ask: Wie heißt du?
You are asking for a name, so open with Wie: Wie heißt du? ('What are you called?').
du is the person being asked (the subject); dich is the object form. Wie heißt du?

activities.prompt: Read the exchange. The first line puts the verb before the person to ask something. Whose name is being asked for?
hints: The opening question uses du, so it addresses the second speaker. Their answer starts with Ich heiße … and gives the name.
activities.feedback: The opening Wie heißt du? asks the second speaker, Leo, for his name, and he answers with the same verb.

errors.explanation: Anna gives her own name in the final line. The opening question asks the second speaker, who answers Ich heiße Leo.
du is the person being asked, not their name. The reply names him: Leo.

activities.body: Ich möchte is the polite 'I would like'. The small surprise is the article: German says ein Kaffee, but once the coffee is what you are ordering, the article becomes einen — Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. Kaffee and Tee are masculine, and a masculine noun takes einen in the object position. Swap the drink and keep the form: einen Tee, bitte. Both drinks are nouns, so both keep their capital letter.

activities.prompt: Which request uses the article German gives a masculine drink when it is the thing being ordered?
hints: Look for the article ending in -en in front of the drink — the object form ein takes with a masculine noun.
activities.feedback: Einen is the form a masculine noun takes as the object being ordered. Ein would leave the coffee standing as a bare subject.

activities.prompt: You are at the counter and coffee is what you want. Make the short request, keeping the article in its object form.
hints: Two words and a polite marker: the object form of 'a' (starts with E) + the drink Kaffee, then bitte.
activities.feedback: Einen Kaffee, bitte — the object form einen survives even in the short request.

errors.explanation: The coffee is the thing being requested, so the masculine article takes the object form: einen Kaffee.
Add bitte to soften the request: Einen Kaffee, bitte.
That full request is correct German — and it comes later in this lesson. This step asks for the short form: Einen Kaffee, bitte.

activities.prompt: The words are shuffled. Build the full polite request for one coffee.
hints: Start with Ich, then the verb möchte in second position, then the object einen Kaffee, and close with bitte.
activities.feedback: The verb möchte comes second and the object einen Kaffee follows it; bitte closes the request.

activities.prompt: Order a tea the same polite way, changing only the drink and keeping the object article.
hints: Copy the coffee request word for word, but swap the drink: Kaffee → Tee. Tee is masculine too, so the article stays einen.
activities.feedback: Same frame, different drink: einen Tee. The article stays einen because Tee is masculine too.

errors.explanation: Tee is masculine, and it is the drink you want, so the article is the object form: einen Tee.
That is the model sentence with the coffee. Change only the drink: Ich möchte einen Tee, bitte.

activities.prompt: Give the English meaning: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte.
hints: möchte is the polite 'would like' — a request, not a statement about liking something in general. bitte is 'please'.
activities.feedback: A request, not a statement about possession: möchte is 'would like'.

answers: I would like a coffee, please.

errors.explanation: Want is closer to German ich will, which is too direct at a counter. möchte is the polite 'would like': I would like a coffee, please.
The German includes möchte — the 'would like' that makes the request polite. Include it: I would like a coffee, please.

activities.prompt: Read the café exchange. Which word marks the drink as the thing being ordered?
hints: Find the article right in front of the drink name — the object form that ends in -en.
activities.feedback: Einen is the object form of the article; the coffee is what is being requested.

errors.explanation: Kaffee is the drink itself. The word that marks it as the thing being ordered is the article before it: einen.
In this exchange the article carries its object ending: einen, not ein.

activities.body: German counts one to ten in two short runs. From twenty upward the system turns around: einundzwanzig is literally 'one-and-twenty', the unit spoken before the ten and joined to it by und. Ask a price with Was kostet? and mind the article: ein Kaffee is the label form of 'one coffee', and the coffee you order becomes einen Kaffee.

activities.prompt: Start on the first run of five. Which German word is the number three?
hints: Count the first run aloud: eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf. The number three is the third word of that run.
activities.feedback: Drei is three, and it sits in the first run, eins to fünf. The second run, sechs to zehn, only begins after that.

activities.prompt: Put the German words in order to ask what one coffee costs.
hints: The question begins with the fixed pair Was kostet ('what costs'), then the thing being priced: ein Kaffee.
activities.feedback: Was kostet goes first as a fixed pair, then the thing being priced. Ein Kaffee here is the label form of 'one coffee'.

activities.prompt: Say in German: Two apples, please.
hints: Number first — zwei — then the plural of Apfel with its capital and umlaut: Äpfel, and close with bitte.
activities.feedback: Äpfel is a noun, so it keeps its capital and takes a plural ending on top of it. The number itself stays zwei.

errors.explanation: One Apfel, two Äpfel: the plural changes a to ä. Write Äpfel with the umlaut.
The prompt asks for two, so the plural is needed: Zwei Äpfel, bitte.
Add the polite bitte to complete the request: Zwei Äpfel, bitte.

activities.prompt: Think: you want one coffee and no price is on the board. Ask the question in German, then write it.
hints: Use the fixed pair Was kostet plus the label form ein Kaffee — the same question you built with the word tiles a moment ago.
activities.feedback: Was kostet asks the price of one thing, and you have just built this question. Say it aloud before you check.

errors.explanation: Here the coffee is the subject of kostet, so it takes the label form ein Kaffee. Einen is for the drink you order: Ich möchte einen Kaffee.

activities.prompt: German's question word takes the front slot and the verb has to follow it. Which of these words is 'where'?
hints: Jonas asks it twice in the story — the word before „ist das Schloss?« and „ist die Toilette?« A question word, not a route word: wo. links, rechts and geradeaus are where the woman's answer points, not questions.
activities.feedback: Wo asks about a place, and it takes the front slot so that ist can take the second. Wer is its counterpart for a person, was for a thing.

activities.prompt: Ask in German where the toilet is. Toilette is feminine.
hints: The second tourist's exact frame: „Entschuldigung, wo ist …?« Only the noun and its article change — die, because Toilette is feminine: Wo ist die Toilette?
activities.feedback: The frame Wo ist does not change; only the noun and its article do, and die marks the feminine Toilette.

errors.explanation: der marks a masculine noun; Toilette is feminine and takes die: Wo ist die Toilette?
das marks a neuter noun; Toilette is feminine and takes die: Wo ist die Toilette?
That is the word order of a subordinate clause. An open question puts the verb second: Wo ist die Toilette?

activities.prompt: Complete the directions: Geradeaus, dann ___
hints: The woman's route was geradeaus, dann links, dann rechts — so after dann comes the middle word, the left turn. Write the direction before the final rechts: links.
activities.feedback: Links is left. Rechts would send you the other way, and it is the word the second step used in the exchange you read.

errors.explanation: rechts is the right turn — the opposite direction. The route goes straight ahead, THEN left: Geradeaus, dann links.
geradeaus is 'straight ahead' — the FIRST direction, before dann. After dann comes the left turn: links.

activities.prompt: German puts the verb straight after the question word. Which of these lines asks what something costs?
hints: The price question starts with Was and puts the verb straight after it: Was kostet… — the other lines ask about health or location.
activities.feedback: Was kostet das? is the price question: Was first, then the verb kostet. Wie geht es? asks after someone's health, and Wo ist das? asks where something is.

activities.prompt: Nicht stands in front of the adjective it cancels. Make «Es ist teuer.» say the opposite.
hints: Keep «Es ist teuer.» as it is and slide nicht in front of teuer: Es ist nicht teuer.
activities.feedback: Es ist nicht teuer puts nicht immediately before teuer; German will not let the nicht drift to the end of the sentence the way English lets the not.

errors.explanation: Nicht belongs directly in front of the adjective it cancels: Es ist nicht teuer — it doesn't drift to the end the way English not does.
The verb ist keeps position two; nicht cancels teuer and stands before it: Es ist nicht teuer.
Billig is 'cheap' — the prompt asks you to negate teuer, not swap the adjective: Es ist nicht teuer.

activities.prompt: You are at a Berlin café counter with a single Kaffee in mind. Ask what it costs.
hints: The coffee stays the subject here (only its price is asked, nothing is ordered), so the article stays ein: Was kostet ein Kaffee?
activities.feedback: Kaffee is masculine and is the subject here, so the article stays ein and the question reads Was kostet ein Kaffee?

errors.explanation: Nothing is being ordered — only the price is asked, so the coffee stays the subject ein: Was kostet ein Kaffee?
Kostet agrees with Kaffee (third person); kostest is the du form: Was kostet ein Kaffee?
The question word opens the w-question: Was kostet ein Kaffee?

activities.prompt: You have finished eating in a German restaurant. Ask for the bill.
hints: Rechnung is feminine, so the article is die — a bare bitte after it turns the phrase into a request: Die Rechnung, bitte.
activities.feedback: Rechnung is feminine, so it takes die, and a bare bitte after it turns the statement into a request.

errors.explanation: Rechnung is feminine — the article is die: Die Rechnung, bitte.
Rechnung is feminine, not neuter: Die Rechnung, bitte.
The bare bitte is what turns the phrase into a polite request: Die Rechnung, bitte.

activities.body: Most German weekdays are a small pantheon. Sonntag and Montag carry the sun and the moon; Dienstag, Donnerstag and Freitag keep the names of old gods, and only Mittwoch names nobody at all — it simply marks the middle of the week. The days are masculine, so ‘on Monday’ is am Montag. And mind the capital letter: morgen is tomorrow, but der Morgen is the morning.

activities.prompt: A Berlin calendar marks each day with one word. Which is the word for today?
hints: Look for the day you are living in right now — heute. The options also include the day after (morgen) and the name of the week itself (Woche).
activities.feedback: Heute is the one. Morgen, Mittwoch and Woche name tomorrow, Wednesday and the week.

activities.prompt: Most German weekdays carry a sun, a moon or a god. Which one names nobody and simply marks the middle of the week?
hints: Think of the literal meaning: mid-week. Donnerstag is named for the god Donar and Sonntag belongs to the sun — only Mittwoch is a plain label for the middle.
activities.feedback: Mittwoch is literally mid-week. Donnerstag thunders with Donar and Sonntag belongs to the sun.

activities.prompt: Read the week. Which day does the passage place in the middle?
hints: The passage says it outright in the fourth sentence: Mittwoch ist die Mitte der Woche. Name that day in German or in English.
activities.feedback: The fourth sentence says it outright: Mittwoch ist die Mitte der Woche.

errors.explanation: Donnerstag thunders for Donar and appears last in the passage as the rainy day. The middle of the week is Mittwoch.
Sonntag opens the passage as the sun's day. Only one sentence calls a day die Mitte der Woche — the one naming Mittwoch.

activities.prompt: Build the German sentence for on Monday I work, with the day in first position.
hints: Open with Am Montag — the day takes the first position — then the verb arbeite, and only after it ich.
activities.feedback: German likes the day in front: Am Montag, then the verb arbeite, then ich.

activities.prompt: Complete with the noun for the morning, not the word for tomorrow: Der ___ ist kalt.
hints: The article Der demands a noun, and German nouns are capitalized. The uncapitalised morgen is the adverb for tomorrow.
activities.feedback: Der Morgen, with the capital letter and the article, is the morning; morgen alone means tomorrow.

segments.text: Complete with the noun for the morning, not the word for tomorrow: Der

errors.explanation: Morgens with -s is the adverb meaning 'in the mornings'. The noun for the morning is der Morgen.
Abend is the evening — the prompt asks for the morning: der Morgen.

activities.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: today is Sunday.
hints: Open with Heute, then ist, then the sun's day — Sonntag, with a capital S.
activities.feedback: Heute ist plus the day. Sonntag is the sun's day, the name sitting in plain sight.

errors.explanation: The line says today is the sun's day — Sonntag — not Montag (Monday).
German keeps the verb in second position after the time word: Heute ist Sonntag.

activities.prompt: Give the English meaning: Am Montag arbeite ich.
hints: Am Montag is 'on Monday'; arbeite ich is 'I work', with the verb pulled up because the day phrase opened the sentence.
activities.feedback: German opens with the day and puts the verb straight after it: am Montag, then arbeite.

errors.explanation: Am means on here — the day phrase keeps its preposition: On Monday I work.
English leads with the time phrase, then subject and verb: On Monday I work.

activities.prompt: All four of these are nouns, so all four wear a capital letter. Which one is the sister?
hints: The sister is die Schwester — the female sibling, not the brother, the parents, or the family itself.
activities.feedback: Schwester is the sister. Bruder is the brother, and Eltern are the parents, with Familie sitting behind all of them.

activities.prompt: You have exactly one brother, and he is the object of your sentence. Predict the form before you write it: I have a brother.
hints: Masculine object → einen: make the one brother the object and the article moves: Ich habe einen Bruder.
activities.feedback: Bruder is masculine and is the direct object, so ein becomes einen: Ich habe einen Bruder.

errors.explanation: Bruder is the masculine object, so ein moves to einen: Ich habe einen Bruder.
Bruder is masculine — the accusative form is einen, not eine: Ich habe einen Bruder.
Schwester is feminine and would stay eine — the sentence is about the brother: Ich habe einen Bruder.

activities.prompt: Bruder is masculine and moves to einen as an object; Schwester does not move. Pick the sentence that says I have a sister.
hints: Schwester is feminine and does not move in the accusative — the article stays eine: Ich habe eine Schwester.
activities.feedback: Schwester is feminine, so the article stays eine in the accusative. Only masculine nouns change, which is why einen Schwester cannot be right.

activities.prompt: Give the sentence a second sister: Ich habe eine Schwester.
hints: Two sisters take the plural noun with -n, and zwei replaces eine: Ich habe zwei Schwestern.
activities.feedback: The plural adds -n to Schwester, and eine becomes zwei: Ich habe zwei Schwestern.

errors.explanation: Zwei takes the plural noun with -n: zwei Schwestern.
Eine is singular — two sisters need zwei plus the plural noun: Ich habe zwei Schwestern.
The prompt adds a second sister, not a brother: Ich habe zwei Schwestern.

activities.prompt: Read the note about a family that has scattered. Which city have the parents stayed in?
hints: The parents' sentence sits at the end of the note — answer with just the city where they stayed: Berlin.
activities.feedback: The last sentence leaves the parents in Berlin while the brother and sister are elsewhere.

errors.explanation: Hamburg is where the brother lives — the parents stayed in Berlin.
Wien is where the sister moved — the parents stayed in Berlin.

activities.prompt: Four everyday nouns, all with a capital letter. Which one is the weather?
hints: The noun that names what the forecast talks about — rain, sun, wind: das Wetter. Zeit is time, Tag is day and Jahr is year — the calendar words around it.
activities.feedback: Wetter is the weather. Zeit is the time, Tag the day and Jahr the year, and all four share the neuter das.

activities.prompt: It is raining, and nobody is doing the raining. Predict the German before you write it: it is raining.
hints: Nobody is doing the raining — German lends the sentence the tiny placeholder es at the front, and the verb takes the -t form: Es regnet.
activities.feedback: German puts the tiny es in front and lets regnen carry the sentence: Es regnet.

errors.explanation: Regnet es? is the question form. The statement starts with the placeholder: Es regnet.
regnen is the infinitive. With the placeholder es, the verb ends in -t: Es regnet.

activities.prompt: Rain needs the tiny es, but the sun acts for itself. Which sentence says the sun is shining?
hints: The sun is the one doing the shining, so it stands before the verb and acts as the subject: Die Sonne scheint. „Es scheint die Sonne« would make the sun the object, and ist + scheinen never combines into a sentence.
activities.feedback: Die Sonne is the subject and scheinen is its verb, so the sun does the shining. Es scheint die Sonne treats the sun as an object and reads wrong.

activities.prompt: The little word that stands in for the whole situation is missing. Fill it in: ___ regnet.
hints: The little placeholder from the story's raining text — the word that stands in for the whole situation with no person involved: Es regnet. (das Wetter would name the noun instead.)
activities.feedback: Es is the placeholder that lets German talk about weather with no subject at all.

segments.text: The little word that stands in for the whole situation is missing. Fill it in:

errors.explanation: das Wetter is the noun 'the weather'. The rain sentence uses the placeholder es alone: Es regnet.
That is the question order. The statement puts the placeholder first: Es regnet.

activities.prompt: Four time words, all feminine. Which one is the time you are free?
hints: The word built from 'free' and 'time' — the hours when you are not working or at school: die Freizeit. Arbeit, Schule and Woche fill the other slots of the week.
activities.feedback: Freizeit is free time. Arbeit is work, Schule is school and Woche is the week; all four take die.

activities.prompt: Say that you like reading. German has no second verb for liking it — predict where the small word goes: I like reading.
hints: German has no 'like + verb' second verb — the small word gern travels with the verb you mean and sits right behind it: Ich lese gern.
activities.feedback: The verb comes second and gern follows it immediately: Ich lese gern.

errors.explanation: The verb must come second; gern follows it: Ich lese gern.
lesen is the infinitive. With ich the verb ends in -e: Ich lese gern.

activities.prompt: Gern travels with the verb, not with the person. Which sentence says I like playing football?
hints: The verb holds second position and gern rides right behind it: Ich spiele gern Fußball. „Ich gern spiele« parks gern before the verb, and „gern nicht« turns it into not liking it.
activities.feedback: The verb holds second position and gern sits behind it. Leading with gern puts the little word where the verb belongs.

activities.prompt: The small word that turns playing into liking it is missing. Fill it in: Ich spiele ___ Fußball.
hints: The small word from the brother's taunt in the story — „Ich spiele gern Tennis!« — the adverb that goes right after the verb: Ich spiele gern Fußball.
activities.feedback: Gern is the whole of German's liking, and it belongs directly behind the verb.

segments.text: The small word that turns playing into liking it is missing. Fill it in: Ich spiele

errors.explanation: nicht would negate the sentence ('I do not play'). The word that says you enjoy playing is gern: Ich spiele gern Fußball.
Tennis is the sport, not the liking-word. The blank asks for the small adverb that means 'like doing': gern.

activities.body: You already know every block you need: the request frame from «At the café» and the introduction from «Introducing yourself». Today you build the sentences yourself, tile by tile. German rule to hold in your head: the verb stands in second position.

activities.prompt: The words are shuffled. Build the full polite request for one coffee.
hints: Verb second: start with Ich, put möchte right behind it, then the drink with its object article, and finish with bitte, comma.
activities.feedback: Ich (1) möchte (2) — the verb holds second position, then the object einen Kaffee, and bitte closes the request.

activities.prompt: Now build the same request for a tea — only the drink changes.
hints: Only the drink changes: swap Kaffee for Tee; Tee is masculine too, so einen stays and the order is identical.
activities.feedback: Only the drink changed: Tee is masculine too, so einen stays.

activities.prompt: Which line follows the German rule — the verb in second position?
hints: The rule is verb-second: check each line for where möchte sits — the verb must be the second block, not the first or the last.
activities.feedback: Only the first line keeps the verb in second position; the others scatter the blocks.

activities.prompt: Build the introduction line you learned in «Introducing yourself».
hints: The same verb-second rule builds introductions too: Ich first, then heiße, then the name.
activities.feedback: Ich (1) heiße (2) Anna — the same verb-second rule builds introductions too.

activities.prompt: The drink is the thing being ordered, so the article takes its object form. Fill the blank.
hints: Kaffee is masculine, and it is the thing being ordered — the object form of ein is einen.
activities.feedback: Einen — Kaffee is masculine, and a masculine object takes einen.

errors.explanation: Ein is the subject form; the drink being ordered takes the object form: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte.
Kaffee is masculine — the object form is einen, not eine (eine is feminine).
That orders a tea — the request here is for Kaffee: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte.

activities.prompt: Say the short version: just the coffee, politely.
hints: Answer with the drink in its object form and the polite word: Einen + Kaffee + comma + bitte.
activities.feedback: Einen Kaffee, bitte. — the object form survives even without the verb.

errors.explanation: The object form survives even without a verb: Einen Kaffee, bitte. Ein is the subject form.
The request names the drink with its object article: Einen Kaffee, bitte.
Kaffee is masculine — the article is einen: Einen Kaffee, bitte.

activities.prompt: Build the friendly line that follows an introduction.
hints: Two blocks only: the verb first, then mich — there is no subject in this friendly line.
activities.feedback: Freut mich. — two blocks, and the verb comes first here because there is no subject at all.

activities.prompt: From memory now: the full polite coffee request.
hints: Everything you built this lesson in one line: Ich + möchte + einen Kaffee + bitte — verb second, object article einen.
activities.feedback: You built it from blocks, and now it is yours: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte.

errors.explanation: The direct object takes the object article: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte.
The request keeps its object article: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte.
Verb-first turns the line into a question; a wish-statement starts with the subject: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte.

activities.body: Your mission: leave the Saturday market with zwei Äpfel, einen Kaffee to take away, and the bill paid — everything in German. You already learned every line you need: the price question from «Prices and paying», the numbers from «Numbers and quantities», the request from «At the café». One step at a time.

activities.prompt: First: ask the price of the apples. Which question does it?
hints: Price questions open with the question word for 'what' — Was. The subject here is plural (zwei Äpfel), so the verb is the plural kosten, not kostet. Wie asks 'how' and Wo asks 'where' — neither starts a price question.
activities.feedback: Was kosten zwei Äpfel? — a plural subject takes kosten; Was kostet is for one thing.

activities.prompt: The seller says: „Zwei Euro.“ You glance at your coins and decide it is a fair price. Complete your verdict with the word from «Prices and paying».
hints: The word from «Prices and paying» for a price that feels fair — 'inexpensive'. It begins with g and is the opposite of teuer: Das ist günstig.
activities.feedback: Günstig — inexpensive. The opposite verdict, teuer, would start a haggle you do not want.

errors.explanation: teuer means 'expensive' — the opposite of your verdict. When two euros feels fair, German says Das ist günstig.
billig also means cheap, but it carries a 'low quality' tone. The positive word for a fair price is günstig.

activities.prompt: The board reads: Apfel 1 Euro, Kaffee 2 Euro. You decide the coffee is the treat and order it to take away. Which line?
hints: Use the same request you made at the café: ich möchte for 'I would like'. The coffee is the thing you order, so the masculine article takes the object form — einen, not ein.
activities.feedback: Einen again — the coffee is the object of your ordering, masculine, so einen.

activities.prompt: You hold the apples and the coffee. Time to pay — but the Rechnung is feminine. Which article?
hints: The bill (die Rechnung) is feminine, and it stays die even when you name it as the thing you want. Capital D, because it opens the sentence.
activities.feedback: Die Rechnung, bitte — feminine noun, so die.

errors.explanation: Rechnung is feminine, so its article is die, not der. Say: Die Rechnung, bitte.
den is the masculine object form; Rechnung is feminine and keeps die: Die Rechnung, bitte.
Eine Rechnung means 'a bill'. Here you want THE bill for your purchase, so German uses the definite article: Die Rechnung, bitte.

activities.prompt: Before the bill arrives, the shopkeeper asks if everything is all right. Answer yes and thank them, the way you learned in your very first lesson.
hints: Your very first lesson gave you the two-word reply: the word for 'yes', then the single word for 'thanks' — the phrase that answers 'everything all right?'
activities.feedback: Ja, danke. — your first German words, still doing work on the mission.

errors.explanation: You said yes, but the friendly question also deserves the thanks: Ja, danke.
bitte asks for something; here you confirm and thank. The answer is Ja, danke.
German puts yes first, then thanks: Ja, danke.

activities.prompt: One for the road: your friend arrives and wants a coffee too. Make the short request.
hints: The three-word request you practiced at the café: the object form of 'a' (Einen), the drink, and bitte — in that order, exactly like your café order.
activities.feedback: Mission complete — Einen Kaffee, bitte, and you walk off the market with everything on the list.

errors.explanation: The coffee is the thing you order, so the masculine article takes the object form: einen Kaffee, not ein Kaffee.
Add bitte — the polite 'please' — to complete the request: Einen Kaffee, bitte.

activities.body: No new words today. This lesson only asks you to remember — each question names the lesson where you learned the answer. Read the refresher above, think before you answer, and trust what you already know.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «At the café»: which article does a masculine drink take when it is being ordered?
hints: The drink is the direct object of möchten — it takes the object form of ein; only one option ends in -en.
activities.feedback: Einen — the object form. Ein would leave the drink standing as a bare subject.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «Prices and paying»: fill the missing first word of the price question.
hints: The price question is a fixed frame: Was … kostet …? — start with the W-word that asks for a price.
activities.feedback: Was kostet das? — the fixed frame for every price question.

errors.explanation: Wie asks how; the price frame is Was kostet das?
Wo asks where; the price frame is Was kostet das?

activities.prompt: You learned this in «First words»: how do you say thank you?
hints: The one-word thank-you, four letters: d-a-n-k-e.
activities.feedback: Danke — still the most useful word you own.

errors.explanation: Danken is the verb 'to thank'; the thanks-word you recall is danke.
Danke alone is the word from «First words»; danke schön is the fuller thanks.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «Asking the way»: you must turn left at the corner. Which word sends you left?
hints: The left-turn word starts with l — the option starting with r sends you the other way.
activities.feedback: Links — rechts would send you the wrong way entirely.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «Days and times»: complete the sentence.
hints: The missing word is the time word for 'today' — it starts with H.
activities.feedback: Heute ist Montag — and morgen it will be Tuesday.

errors.explanation: Morgen is tomorrow; the sentence says it is Monday now — Heute ist Montag.
Gestern is yesterday; the sentence means today — Heute ist Montag.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «Family and people»: write the German for “the brother”.
hints: Masculine noun plus its article: der + Bruder.
activities.feedback: Der Bruder — masculine, so der.

errors.explanation: Bruder is masculine — its article is der: der Bruder.
Bruder is masculine — its article is der, not das (neuter).
That is the sister (die Schwester); the brother is der Bruder.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «Weather and seasons»: which line says it is raining?
hints: The raining line uses the verb regnen — only one option has it.
activities.feedback: Es regnet. — if the sun were out, the second line would be the one.

activities.prompt: You learned this in «Free time and hobbies»: complete the line with the little word that means “gladly”.
hints: The little adverb that means 'gladly / like to' has four letters: g-e-r-n.
activities.feedback: Gern — the little word that turns playing into liking to play.

errors.explanation: The blank is not the verb — the verb stays in its ich-form spiele: Ich spiele gern Fußball.
Lieber is 'rather/preferably'; the word for 'gladly' is gern.

activities.body: Your mission: it is tomorrow morning and you are at München Hauptbahnhof — Munich's main station. Your train to Hamburg leaves soon, and you need three things: a ticket, the price, and the platform. The key phrases are below. Read each out loud once. Notice how everything you have learned clicks together here: ich möchte to ask for things, wo for where, links and rechts for directions. Same words, brand-new adventure.

activities.prompt: You reach the ticket counter. The clerk looks up and asks: Wohin? — Where to? What do you say?
hints: The clerk asked where you are going — Wohin? (Where to?). Answer with the destination: the word for 'to' that pairs with a city (nach), the city, and bitte.
activities.feedback: Nach Hamburg, bitte. — nach means to when a city follows, and bitte softens every request. You have told them exactly where you are going.

activities.prompt: Now ask for the ticket itself. Write in German: I would like a ticket.
hints: The same polite opener you used for coffee — ich möchte — then the ticket. Fahrkarte is feminine, so the object-form article is eine.
activities.feedback: Ich möchte eine Fahrkarte. — the same ich möchte you used for coffee, now buying a train ticket. The words travel with you.

errors.explanation: Fahrkarte is feminine, so the object-form article is eine: Ich möchte eine Fahrkarte.
einen is the masculine object form; Fahrkarte is feminine, so eine: Ich möchte eine Fahrkarte.
Karte is a card; the ticket you buy at the station is die Fahrkarte.

activities.prompt: The clerk nods: one ticket to Hamburg. Before you pay, you need the price. What do you ask?
hints: You need a price, and the line for that is the question word 'what' plus the verb 'to cost' — Was kostet …? The very line you used at the market.
activities.feedback: Was kostet das? — how much does that cost? The exact line you used at the market. Prices are prices, everywhere.

activities.prompt: The clerk answers with the price. Complete the sentence:
hints: The price is one of the numbers from «Numbers and quantities» — the one that means 10, written as a word.
activities.feedback: Das kostet zehn Euro. — zehn is one of the six-through-ten numbers you learned. Say the whole sentence out loud: it sounds like a real traveler.

errors.explanation: Euro is already in the sentence — the blank takes just the number: Das kostet zehn Euro.
Write the German number in letters: zehn, not the digit 10.

activities.prompt: Build your full request at the counter. Say: I would like a ticket, please.
hints: Build the request in one breath: the polite opener Ich, the verb möchte, the ticket with its feminine article (eine Fahrkarte), and bitte closing with a comma and period.
activities.feedback: Ich möchte eine Fahrkarte, bitte. — the whole request in one breath. The clerk is already printing your ticket.

activities.prompt: Ticket in hand. Now the platform: where is Gleis vier? What do you ask the guard?
hints: You are asking where the platform is — the question word wo ('where'), the platform Gleis vier, and bitte to ask politely.
activities.feedback: Wo ist Gleis vier, bitte? — wo for where, bitte for warmth. Gleis means platform, and right now it is the most important word in the station.

activities.prompt: The guard points down the hall. Complete the directions:
hints: The direction that follows 'straight ahead' — the word for 'right' from your directions lesson. It is the opposite of links.
activities.feedback: Geradeaus, dann rechts. — straight ahead, then right. The direction words you learned are doing the whole job here.

errors.explanation: links is 'left'. The guard said straight ahead, then right: rechts.
Just rechts after dann — nach is not needed here: geradeaus, dann rechts.

activities.prompt: The train to Hamburg rolls in. You turn to the guard with a smile. Write it in German: Thank you!
hints: The one word for 'thank you' — the one you used after your coffee. Capital letter, full stop, mission done.
activities.feedback: Danke. — and you are aboard, ticket in hand, platform found. Mission complete.

errors.explanation: Vielen Dank is the longer 'many thanks'. The line this step practices is the short Danke.
Danke schön is 'thank you very much' — a real phrase, but this step asks for the plain Danke.

activities.body: Your mission: it is Sunday afternoon and you are on the doorstep of your friend Lena's house in Hamburg. Her parents open the door. You get exactly one first impression: a greeting, your name, and warmth. The lines that carry the whole evening are below — read each out loud. Notice the pattern you already know: the greeting always comes first, then your name, then something kind.

activities.prompt: The door opens. Lena's parents smile at you. What leaves your mouth first?
hints: The greeting opens every exchange — the word you say the moment the door opens, before your name, before anything else. It is the very first German word you learned.
activities.feedback: Hallo first — always. The greeting opens every door in Germany, literally this time.

activities.prompt: Write in German: My name is Anna.
hints: German gives a name with the verb 'to be called' — heißen — not with sein. With ich it becomes heiße, then your name: Ich heiße Anna.
activities.feedback: Ich heiße Anna. — ich heiße is I am called, the German way to give your name. Now say it with your own name.

errors.explanation: Ich bin Anna says 'I am Anna' with sein. The step asks for the verb 'to be called': Ich heiße Anna.
ich takes heiße; heißt is the du-form. Pair ich with heiße: Ich heiße Anna.
The introduction names you — end with your name: Ich heiße Anna.

activities.prompt: Lena's mother beams: Hallo Anna! You answer warmly:
hints: Two words answer a warm 'Hallo Anna!' — the phrase that means literally 'it pleases me'. It is the friendly reply that keeps the conversation warm.
activities.feedback: Freut mich. — nice to meet you. Two words that make any German host smile. Directions and prices can wait for another day.

activities.prompt: Introduce your sister. Build: My sister is called Lena.
hints: Order: the possessive Meine, the family word Schwester, the same verb you used for your own name (heißt), and her name at the end.
activities.feedback: Meine Schwester heißt Lena. — meine is my, and heißt does the same job as in ich heiße. You are introducing a whole family now.

activities.prompt: At the table, Lena's father asks what you enjoy doing. You want to say you like playing. What do you answer?
hints: To say you like doing something, German puts the verb in the ich-form and adds gern — 'with pleasure'. The other options glue a politeness word onto the verb, which changes nothing.
activities.feedback: Ich spiele gern. — gern turns any verb into a like: ich spiele gern is I like playing. Bitte and danke are lovely words, but they are not hobbies.

activities.prompt: Lena's mother asks about your family. Complete your answer:
hints: The masculine family word that means 'brother' — it pairs with Mein (masculine 'my'), while your sister would take Meine.
activities.feedback: Mein Bruder wohnt in Hamburg. — my brother lives in Hamburg. Mein pairs with masculine words like Bruder, and wohnt is lives, right from your free-time lesson.

errors.explanation: Schwester is feminine and would need Meine, not Mein. The word for a brother is Bruder.
Brüder is the plural ('brothers'), but wohnt is singular. One brother: Bruder.

activities.prompt: It is late and you have to go. At the door, you thank the family for the evening. What do you say?
hints: The single word that closes a German evening — the thanks you used at the café. Not a direction, not a price: Danke.
activities.feedback: Danke. — thank you. A small word with big warmth; it is how you close an evening in Germany.

activities.prompt: The whole visit in one line. Write in German: Hello, my name is Anna.
hints: Two pieces from this lesson, in their order: the greeting, a comma, then the ich-heiße introduction with your name.
activities.feedback: Hallo, ich heiße Anna. — greeting, name, warmth, exactly as you practiced. Lena's parents are smiling. Mission complete.

errors.explanation: Introductions use the verb 'to be called', not sein: Hallo, ich heiße Anna.
The greeting opens the line: Hallo, ich heiße Anna.

activities.body: This lesson is pure building. You already know the words — heute, morgen, Montag, gern, spielen, wohnen. Now you will stack them into real German sentences. One pattern to notice before you start: when a sentence begins with a time word, the verb comes second. Heute spiele ich — today play I. It feels backwards, then suddenly it does not. Read the examples below out loud.

activities.prompt: Build: Today I play.
hints: Time first, then the verb, then the person: Heute + spiele + ich.
activities.feedback: Heute spiele ich. — time first, verb second. Feel that rhythm; it never changes.

activities.prompt: Build: I like playing.
hints: Ich + the verb, then the little word for 'gladly' at the end — gern.
activities.feedback: Ich spiele gern. — gern after the verb turns it into a like. One tiny word, a whole new meaning.

activities.prompt: Which sentence has true German word order?
hints: With a time word first, the verb still jumps to second position — only one line does that.
activities.feedback: Morgen ist kalt. — tomorrow it is cold. Time first, verb second: the pattern holds again.

activities.prompt: Start a sentence with a day word. Complete it:
hints: The day-word that means 'tomorrow' — it starts with M and ends in -gen. Put it first, before ist.
activities.feedback: Morgen ist Montag. — tomorrow is Monday. You just built a sentence about the week.

errors.explanation: Heute is today; the sentence is about tomorrow — Morgen ist Montag.
Gestern is yesterday; the sentence says tomorrow is Monday — Morgen ist Montag.

activities.prompt: Build: The family likes playing.
hints: Die + Familie, then the verb form for one family, then gern at the end.
activities.feedback: Die Familie spielt gern. — four tiles, one real sentence about real people.

activities.prompt: Write in German: I live in Berlin.
hints: Ich + the verb for living somewhere (wohnen) + in + the city.
activities.feedback: Ich wohne in Berlin. — wohnen is to live somewhere. Another brick in your week.

errors.explanation: Leben means to be alive; living in a place is wohnen: Ich wohne in Berlin.
Wohnen takes the preposition in before the place: Ich wohne in Berlin.
After ich the verb takes -e: Ich wohne in Berlin.

activities.prompt: Talk about your sister's hobbies. Complete it:
hints: One sister, one person — the verb form ends in -t: spielt, not spiele.
activities.feedback: Meine Schwester spielt gern. — my sister likes playing. Spielt, not spiele — the verb changes with the person, and you just handled it.

errors.explanation: Spiele is the ich-form; with meine Schwester (one person, sie) the verb is spielt.
Spielen is the infinitive or the wir/sie-plural form; with meine Schwester use spielt.

activities.prompt: Final test — the whole pattern in one choice. Which is correct German?
hints: The pattern you built all lesson: time first, verb second, person after the verb.
activities.feedback: Heute spiele ich. — time, verb, person. You have built real sentences all lesson; this pattern is yours now.

activities.body: Every German noun has a gender, and you can see it in the article: der Tisch, die Küche, das Zimmer. The indefinite article splits the same way — ein Tisch, eine Küche, ein Zimmer. Ein goes with masculine and neuter nouns; eine goes only with feminine nouns. Learn every noun together with its article, because the gender is part of the word.

activities.prompt: Which one is the kitchen?
hints: The kitchen is a feminine noun that takes die. The two masculine options are Tisch and Stuhl, and Bett is neuter — only one option carries die.
activities.feedback: Küche is feminine, so it takes die: die Küche. Tisch and Stuhl are masculine (der), Bett is neuter (das).
