Then comes das Vorstellungsgespräch — the interview — plus das Gehalt and der Lebenslauf. Six words, and you can read a German job ad.

activities.prompt: Which means 'the job interview'?
hints: The interview is the long compound das Vorstellungsgespräch — Stelle is the position and Beruf the profession.
activities.feedback: Das Vorstellungsgespräch. Die Stelle is the position, der Beruf the profession.

activities.prompt: Predict and write: The interview is on Monday.
hints: Das Vorstellungsgespräch + ist + am Montag — am is the weekday preposition.
activities.feedback: Das Vorstellungsgespräch ist am Montag.

errors.explanation: Weekdays take am, not in: am Montag.
Gespräch is neuter — the article is das: das Vorstellungsgespräch.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
hints: Bewerben must keep both mich and um — the other options drop mich, use mir, or scramble the order.
activities.feedback: Ich bewerbe mich um eine Stelle — bewerben needs mich + um. The others drop or scramble the mich.

options.text: Ich bewerbe mich um eine Stelle.
Ich bewerbe mir um eine Stelle.
Ich mich bewerbe um eine Stelle.

activities.prompt: Arrange the words: I am applying for a position.
hints: Ich bewerbe, then mich um, then eine Stelle — bewerben needs the reflexive mich plus um.
activities.feedback: Ich bewerbe mich um eine Stelle.

activities.prompt: Say it with bewerben: Ich will die Stelle.
hints: Rebuild the sentence with the reflexive verb: Ich bewerbe mich um die Stelle.
activities.feedback: Ich bewerbe mich um die Stelle.

answers: Ich bewerbe mich um die Stelle.

errors.explanation: Bewerben needs the reflexive mich: Ich bewerbe mich um die Stelle.

errors.answer: Ich bewerbe mir um die Stelle.
errors.explanation: Mir is the dative 'to me' — the reflexive for bewerben is mich: Ich bewerbe mich um die Stelle.

activities.prompt: Complete the application: Ich bewerbe mich ___ eine Stelle als Lehrer.
hints: Bewerben always comes as bewerben + mich + um: Ich bewerbe mich um eine Stelle.
activities.feedback: Um: Ich bewerbe mich um eine Stelle als Lehrer.

segments.text: Complete the application: Ich bewerbe mich

errors.explanation: Applying for a job is sich bewerben um — für ('for') is not the preposition bewerben takes.
Bei means 'at/with' a company; the application formula is sich bewerben um eine Stelle.

activities.prompt: Read the job ad. What should you send?
hints: The polite instruction in the ad names the thing to send — answer with exactly that.
activities.feedback: Ihren Lebenslauf — your CV.

errors.explanation: Das Gehalt is the salary the ad calls good — what you send is Ihren Lebenslauf.
Die Stelle is the position being offered, not the thing to send — send Ihren Lebenslauf.

activities.body: Your mission: a job interview — in German. The interviewer will ask about you, your experience, and your plans. You have everything you need: würde for polite wishes (Ich würde gern hier arbeiten), Perfekt for experience (Ich habe ... gearbeitet), Futur for plans (Ich werde viel lernen), and Könnten Sie...? for polite questions. Read the four model sentences below out loud, then walk in.

activities.prompt: The interviewer smiles: 'Erzählen Sie etwas über sich.' What do you say first?
hints: Answer the invitation to introduce yourself ('Erzählen Sie etwas über sich') with the polite wish you practiced: Ich würde gern … — 'I would like to…'. The other options sidestep the interview.
activities.feedback: Ich würde gern hier arbeiten — polite, on-topic, in German. The goal, right away.

activities.prompt: Describe your experience: I worked in Berlin for three years.
hints: Perfekt wraps the sentence: Ich habe first, the time phrase drei Jahre, the place in Berlin, and the past participle gearbeitet last. The participle stays at the end.
activities.feedback: Ich habe drei Jahre in Berlin gearbeitet — Perfekt for experience.

activities.prompt: Ask politely: Could you please repeat that?
hints: The infinitive that means 'to repeat' — it comes after bitte at the end of the polite question. It starts with w- and contains the word for 'again', wieder: wiederholen.
activities.feedback: Wiederholen — 'to repeat': Könnten Sie das bitte wiederholen?

segments.text: Complete politely: Könnten Sie das bitte

errors.explanation: After Könnten Sie the main verb stays in the infinitive: wiederholen, not the participle wiederholt.
wieder is 'again' on its own. The verb that means 'to repeat' is wiederholen.

activities.prompt: They ask about your plans. Which answer uses the future?
hints: Plans use the future: the auxiliary werden in the ich-form (werde) with the infinitive at the end. Würde expresses a wish, habe gelernt is the past, and lerne is the present.
activities.feedback: Ich werde viel lernen — werden + infinitive is the future. Würde is a wish, habe gelernt is the past.

activities.prompt: Close the interview with thanks: Thank you for the interview.
hints: Build the closing thanks: a thanks phrase (Vielen Dank), then für, then the neuter noun Gespräch with its article das.
activities.feedback: Vielen Dank für das Gespräch — and the job is practically yours.

errors.explanation: Gespräch is neuter, so the article is das: für das Gespräch, not die.
Gespräch is neuter, so the article is das: für das Gespräch, not der.

activities.body: Your mission: tonight you're cooking dinner, and the market closes soon. Buy ein Kilo Äpfel, eine Flasche Wasser and ein Stück Käse — everything in German. You already learned every line you need in «At the market»: the amount words, Ich nehme…, and gern for your favorite. The list is below. Los geht's!

activities.prompt: The stall owner asks what you'd like. Which line says you'll take a piece of cheese?
hints: The market formula again: Ich nehme ein Stück Käse — the amount with its neuter article (ein Stück), then the food Käse at the end.
activities.feedback: Stück is neuter, so ein Stück — and nehmen carries the purchase: Ich nehme ein Stück Käse.

activities.body: Your mission: your head is pounding and the Apotheke closes in twenty minutes. Get etwas gegen Kopfschmerzen — everything in German. You learned the tools in «At the pharmacy»: brauchen for needing, gegen for against, Tablette and Medikament. Walk in and ask.

activities.prompt: The pharmacist looks up. Which line asks for something for a headache?
hints: The phrase from this lesson: Ich brauche etwas gegen Kopfschmerzen — 'something for headaches'. Watch the preposition gegen and the plural Kopfschmerzen at the end.
activities.feedback: Etwas keeps it usefully vague and gegen names the enemy: Ich brauche etwas gegen Kopfschmerzen.

activities.body: Your mission: your friend has fallen on the stairs and can't get up. Call for help, tell someone to call the doctor, and give the emergency number — everything in German, fast. You learned the tools in «Emergencies»: Hilfe!, the formal command Rufen Sie…, and 112. Go.

Saturday night, your kitchen. You're calling your friend Anna to invite her to your birthday party. She'll hesitate — work, maybe — and you'll need charm with grammar: einladen splits in two, Ja, gern! says yes, and am Samstag pins the day. The key lines are below. Say them out loud once, then pick up the phone.

activities.prompt: Anna: „Deine Party klingt toll! Aber ich arbeite am Samstag…“ — She sounds unsure. Which reply keeps the invitation alive?
hints: Keep the door open — push past her doubt with the invitation itself: Komm doch trotzdem — ich lade dich herzlich ein!
activities.feedback: Komm doch! keeps the door open and einladen names the invitation. Giving up, or declining on her behalf, ends the conversation.

options.text: Komm doch trotzdem — ich lade dich herzlich ein!
Dann lade ich dich nicht ein.

activities.prompt: Anna: „Na gut — wann denn genau?“ — Pin it down:
hints: Pin the day with am Samstag, then confirm: Am Samstag. Kommst du?
activities.feedback: Am Samstag pins the day and Kommst du? asks the question. Vague answers lose the plan.

activities.body: Monday morning, the waiting room. Your Kopf has hurt since yesterday and your Arm feels strange. The doctor will ask where it hurts — answer the German way: pain happens to you, Mir tut … weh. The key lines are below. Say them out loud once, then go in.

activities.prompt: Doctor: „Was fehlt Ihnen?“ — Tell her your head hurts, the German way:
hints: German lets the pain happen to you: Mir tut der Kopf weh. Mein Kopf tut weh is English wearing a German coat.
activities.feedback: Pain happens to you: Mir tut der Kopf weh. Mein Kopf tut weh is English wearing a German coat.

activities.prompt: Doctor: „Seit wann?“ — Since yesterday:
hints: Seit plus a point in time means since: Seit gestern. Für means for and ab means from.
activities.feedback: Seit plus a time means since: Seit gestern. The doctor nods and writes it down.

activities.body: Evening, a small hotel in Hamburg. The receptionist is friendly but busy. You need a quiet room, the window opened, and the Wi-Fi code. In German, politeness has a grammar: Könnten Sie…? Wäre es möglich…? Add bitte, keep the infinitive at the end. The key lines are below — read them out loud once, then step up to the desk.

activities.prompt: Receptionist: „Guten Abend! Was kann ich für Sie tun?“ — Ask for a quiet room, politely:
hints: The polite frame is Könnten Sie … bitte …? with the infinitive last: Könnten Sie mir bitte ein ruhiges Zimmer geben?
activities.feedback: Könnten Sie bitte…? is the polite frame. Demands and blunt wollen don't open doors — soft questions do.

options.text: Könnten Sie mir bitte ein ruhiges Zimmer geben?

activities.prompt: Receptionist: „Sehr gern. Sonst noch etwas?“ — Ask whether opening the window is possible:
hints: Wäre es möglich …? is the softest frame for a request at a front desk.
activities.feedback: Wäre es möglich…? is the softest frame in German. A command at a front desk lands badly.

options.text: Wäre es möglich, das Fenster zu öffnen?

activities.body: Friday evening, a friend's party in Berlin. You don't know anyone — perfect. German small talk runs on w-questions: wer, was, wo, wann. Question word first, verb second. Ask, listen, ask again. The key lines are below — then walk over to the stranger by the window.

activities.prompt: You: „Hallo! Ich bin Alex.“ — Stranger: „Hallo! Freut mich.“ — Ask where she lives:
hints: Question word first, verb second with the du ending: Wo wohnst du?
activities.feedback: Question word first, verb second: Wo wohnst du? The verb must follow wo immediately.

activities.prompt: Stranger: „In Kreuzberg. Und du?“ — „In Mitte.“ — „Was machst du beruflich?“ — Answer, and keep the chat going:
hints: Answer with the verb in second position, then toss the question back: Ich arbeite als Lehrer. Und du?
activities.feedback: Answer, then return the question: Und du? is the little engine of small talk.

options.text: Ich arbeite als Lehrer. Und du?

activities.body: Sunday lunch at your partner's parents' house in München. They ask about your Familie — Bruder, Schwester, Eltern. Give every relative the right article, and remember the accusative rule: masculine objects move to einen, the rest stay. The key lines are below. Tief durchatmen — then charm them.

activities.prompt: Mother: „Erzähl mal — hast du Geschwister?“ — Say you have a brother:
hints: Brother is the masculine object, so the article moves to einen: Ich habe einen Bruder. Only the article moves.
activities.feedback: Bruder is masculine and the object: einen Bruder. Only the masculine article moves.

activities.prompt: Father: „Und deine Eltern — wo wohnen sie?“ — Answer:
hints: Eltern is plural, so the verb takes the plural form and the possessive is meine: Meine Eltern wohnen in Berlin.
activities.feedback: Eltern is plural: meine Eltern wohnen. The verb must agree with the plural subject.

activities.body: Sunday morning, the Flohmarkt in Berlin. A leather bag catches your eye — 40 euros, the tag says. Too much. Ask the price, wince politely (Das ist zu teuer), and make your offer. In German the price question never changes: Was kostet das? The key lines are below.

activities.prompt: Seller: „Das ist ein schönes Stück — echtes Leder!“ — Ask what it costs:
hints: The price question is a fixed frame: Was kostet das? — Was first, then the verb, then das. The other options break that frame.
activities.feedback: Was kostet das? — question word, verb second. The frame never changes, whatever the price.

activities.prompt: The seller says 35. You want the polite word for 'inexpensive' — the one a shopkeeper won't wince at. Which is it?
hints: The shopkeeper-safe word for inexpensive is günstig — billig can sound like cheap junk and kostenlos means free.
activities.feedback: Günstig means inexpensive without insulting the goods. Billig can sound cheap in the bad way — never about someone's leather bag.

activities.prompt: Seller: „40 Euro.“ — Too expensive. React, and offer 25:
hints: Name the problem with zu teuer, then put your counter-price as a question: Das ist zu teuer. 25 Euro?
activities.feedback: Das ist zu teuer names the problem; naming your price keeps the haggle alive. Zu billig means the opposite of what you want.

activities.prompt: Arrange the words: I cooked yesterday.
hints: Ich + habe, then gestern, and the participle gekocht last — helper second, participle last.
activities.feedback: Ich habe gestern gekocht — haben second, the participle last, the time word in the middle.

activities.prompt: Arrange the words: you will travel soon.
hints: Du takes wirst (werden's du-form), then the time word bald, and the infinitive last.
activities.feedback: Du wirst bald reisen — werden conjugated in second position, the infinitive parked at the very end.

activities.prompt: Arrange the words: that is the woman who lives there.
hints: Das ist die Frau, then the pronoun die (copying die Frau), then dort — and wohnt at the end of the clause.
activities.feedback: Das ist die Frau, die dort wohnt — the pronoun copies die Frau, and wohnt slides to the end of the clause.

activities.prompt: Arrange the words: the chairs are new.
hints: Die plural article, then the plural Stühle with its umlaut, then sind, then neu.
activities.feedback: Die Stühle sind neu — die for every plural, sind for the plural verb, and the umlaut is part of the plural.

activities.prompt: Arrange the words: I have no time.
hints: Ich + habe + the negating article for feminine Zeit (keine) + Zeit.
activities.feedback: Ich habe keine Zeit — Zeit is feminine, so keine. The noun decides which negator you build with.

activities.body: No new words today — this lesson only asks you to remember. You learned this in «Perfekt with haben» — haben plus participle. Then came the twist: movement and change take sein. Ich bin gegangen, du bist gekommen.. Read the refresher below, think before you answer, and trust what you already know.

activities.prompt: Complete with the right helper: Wir ___ gestern geblieben.
hints: Bleiben (to stay, a change of place) takes sein — and wir takes sind.
activities.feedback: Bleiben is a change of place, so it takes sein: Wir sind gestern geblieben. Haben would be wrong here.

segments.text: Complete with the right helper: Wir

errors.explanation: Bleiben is a change of place — it takes sein, not haben: Wir sind gestern geblieben.
Seid is the ihr-form; with wir the helper is sind.

activities.body: No new words today — this lesson only asks you to remember. You learned this in «Yesterday: a first look at the past» — haben plus the participle. Now the storyteller's shortcut: war, hatte, konnte, musste. One word instead of two.. Read the refresher below, think before you answer, and trust what you already know.

activities.prompt: Complete the story opening: Es ___ einmal ein kleines Café.
hints: The fairy-tale opener runs on sein's story past: Es war einmal …
activities.feedback: Es war einmal — 'once upon a time' runs on war, the Präteritum of sein.

errors.explanation: Ist is the present; the story opener needs the past war: Es war einmal.
Hatte is 'had'; the opener is Es war einmal.

activities.body: No new words today — this lesson only asks you to remember. You learned this in «Würde: wishes and polite would» — the soft would. Now its daydreaming cousin: Ich wünschte, ich wäre… — wishes that need their own grammar.. Read the refresher below, think before you answer, and trust what you already know.

activities.prompt: Complete the wish: Ich wünschte, ich ___ in Italien.
hints: The unreal form of sein — wäre. Wünschte sets the wish up, wäre delivers it.
activities.feedback: Wäre — the unreal form of sein. Wünschen sets it up, wäre delivers it.

segments.text: Complete the wish: Ich wünschte, ich

errors.explanation: Bin is the real form; the wish needs the unreal wäre.
War is the plain past; the unreal form of sein is wäre.
Würde pairs with an infinitive; after wünschte the unreal sein is wäre.

activities.body: No new words today — this lesson only asks you to remember. You learned this in «Komparativ: bigger, better» — schneller, besser, mehr. Now crown the winner: am schnellsten, der beste.. Read the refresher below, think before you answer, and trust what you already know.

activities.prompt: Complete the winner: Er läuft ___.
hints: No noun follows, so the standalone form: am + schnellsten.
activities.feedback: Am schnellsten — am plus -sten when the superlative stands alone.

errors.explanation: The standalone superlative ends in -sten: am schnellsten.
Schnell is the plain adjective; the winner's form is am schnellsten.
Der + -ste needs a noun after it; standing alone it is am schnellsten.

activities.body: No new words today — this lesson only asks you to remember. You learned this in «Days and times» — the days, the hours, the numbers. Now the twist Germans love: halb drei means half past two, because German looks forward to the coming hour.. Read the refresher below, think before you answer, and trust what you already know.

activities.prompt: Complete the time: Es ist viertel ___ acht.
hints: Quarter PAST the hour is viertel nach — vor would look back to the hour before.
activities.feedback: Viertel nach acht — quarter past eight. Nach looks forward, vor looks back.

segments.text: Complete the time: Es ist viertel

errors.explanation: Vor looks back to the previous hour; quarter PAST eight is viertel nach acht.
Um means at (a clock time); the quarter-hour phrase is viertel nach acht.

activities.body: No new words today — this lesson only asks you to remember. You learned this in «At the café» — Ich möchte einen Kaffee. Now the full toolkit: können and möchten, with the main verb parked at the very end.. Read the refresher below, think before you answer, and trust what you already know.

activities.prompt: Complete the request: Ich ___ Deutsch sprechen.
hints: The ich-form of the modal 'can' — kann — goes second; sprechen already waits at the end.
activities.feedback: Ich kann Deutsch sprechen — the modal in second position, sprechen last.

errors.explanation: With ich the modal is kann: Ich kann Deutsch sprechen.
Kannst is the du-form; with ich the modal is kann.
Sprechen is already at the end of the line — the blank holds the modal kann.

activities.body: Jonas has exactly one hour in Heidelberg, and he is already lost. The castle is somewhere above him, the old bridge somewhere below. He stops a woman with a dog. »Entschuldigung — wo ist das Schloss?«
»Geradeaus, dann links«, she says, pointing up the hill. »Und dann rechts — das Schloss ist groß, Sie können es nicht verpassen.« Jonas repeats it like a spell: geradeaus, dann links, dann rechts.
Twenty minutes later Jonas stands in front of the castle, out of breath and grinning. A tourist asks him: »Entschuldigung, wo ist die Toilette?« Jonas smiles. Now he knows this one.

activities.prompt: Jonas repeats the route under his breath. Which word means 'straight ahead'?
hints: The route's first word — the one the woman said before „dann links«: geradeaus. links and rechts are the turns that come after dann, and wo asks a question.
activities.feedback: Geradeaus is straight ahead — the first word of almost every route. Links and rechts come after dann.

activities.prompt: Write in German the first two directions Jonas heard: Straight ahead, then left.
hints: The first two words of the woman's route, in order — the straight-ahead word first, then the left turn after dann, with a comma before dann: Geradeaus, dann links.
activities.feedback: Geradeaus, dann links: the first two directions to the castle.

errors.explanation: rechts is the right turn — but the woman's route turns LEFT after straight ahead: Geradeaus, dann links. (rechts came later, after the castle gate.)
The route starts straight ahead first, then turns left: Geradeaus, dann links — not the other way round.

activities.body: Friday evening, Hamburg. Lena plans a picnic at the Alster for Saturday — sun, blankets, friends. The forecast says: »Morgen scheint die Sonne.« She believes it.
Saturday morning: grey sky, cold wind. »Es regnet«, texts her friend. »Es ist kalt!« Lena looks out the window. In Hamburg regnet es heute den ganzen Tag — or so it seems.
By afternoon the clouds break. Die Sonne scheint, aber es ist kalt. Lena grabs a jacket and goes anyway. The picnic happens — with hot tea instead of lemonade.

activities.prompt: Write in German: The sun is shining, but it is cold.
hints: Join the two weather sentences from the story with aber: the sun part first, then the cold part — which needs its own placeholder es: Die Sonne scheint, aber es ist kalt.
activities.feedback: Die Sonne scheint, aber es ist kalt: the picnic needs a jacket.

answers: Die Sonne scheint, aber es ist kalt.

errors.answer: Es scheint die Sonne, aber es ist kalt.
errors.explanation: The sun acts for itself in this lesson, so it is the subject: Die Sonne scheint, aber es ist kalt.

errors.answer: Die Sonne scheint, aber ist kalt.
errors.explanation: The cold part needs its own subject placeholder: Die Sonne scheint, aber es ist kalt.

activities.body: Tim and his brother have a bet: who spends Saturday better? Tim says: »Ich lese gern.« His brother laughs: »Lesen? Ich spiele gern Tennis!« The bet is on.
Saturday comes. Tim reads on the sofa — three chapters, very proud. His brother plays tennis with friends, then texts: »Wir spielen gern Tennis — komm doch!« Tim looks at his book. Then at the sun.
Tim goes. He loses every game, laughs the whole time, and stays for dinner. On Sunday his brother asks: »Und — was war besser?« Tim grins.

activities.prompt: Write Tim’s new answer in German: I like playing tennis.
hints: Tim switches sides for the bet — his brother's sport, in the same verb + gern order he just learned: Ich spiele gern Tennis.
activities.feedback: Ich spiele gern Tennis: Tim has changed his mind about Saturdays.

errors.explanation: The verb holds second position and gern comes after it: Ich spiele gern Tennis.
That is the OLD answer from the bet — his brother's line. Tim's new line switches to Tennis.
The sentence is about the sport of the bet: Ich spiele gern Tennis.

activities.body: 22:40, München Hauptbahnhof. Anna's train to Berlin leaves in twenty minutes — Gleis 11, probably. She runs. A man with a suitcase runs faster.
»Entschuldigung — wo ist Gleis 11?« The man points: »Geradeaus, dann links.« Anna runs. Her ticket says Wagen 7, Platz 42. The train is long, the night is cold.
She finds Wagen 7 at 22:58. The doors close behind her. From the window, Munich slides away. »Endlich«, she texts. »Ich fahre mit dem Zug nach Berlin.«

activities.prompt: Write Anna’s message in German: I am in Berlin.
hints: Anna's text to her phone — the being-verb with ich: Ich bin in Berlin. fahren would still be travelling; she has arrived.
activities.feedback: Ich bin in Berlin: Anna made the train.

errors.explanation: haben means possession, not location. Being somewhere uses sein: Ich bin in Berlin.
fahren says you are still travelling; Anna's message says she ARRIVED: Ich bin in Berlin.

activities.body: »Was hast du gestern gemacht?« asks the teacher. Paul thinks fast. The truth: he played games until midnight. The answer he gives: »Ich habe viel gelernt.«
The teacher smiles. »Und gegessen? Was hast du gegessen?« Paul: »Ich habe Brot gegessen und Wasser getrunken.« True, at least — at 2 a.m., between games.
»Und deine Schwester?« Paul grins: »Meine Schwester hat gearbeitet.« The class laughs. Someone always worked — just not Paul.

activities.prompt: Write Paul’s honest answer in German: I played.
hints: Paul's honest Saturday, in the same perfect frame: spielen's regular participle gespielt at the end — Ich habe gespielt.
activities.feedback: Ich habe gespielt: that is what Paul really did.

errors.explanation: spielen is the infinitive. The perfect participle ends in -t: Ich habe gespielt.
habe keeps second position; the participle goes last: Ich habe gespielt.

activities.body: »Was hast du am Wochenende gemacht?« On Monday everyone asks. Maria decides to tell it properly — with signposts: zuerst, dann, danach, am Ende.
Zuerst hat sie lange geschlafen. Dann ist sie spazieren gegangen — drei Stunden, durch den Park. Danach hat sie ihre Freunde getroffen: Kaffee, Kuchen, viel Lachen.
Am Ende haben sie zusammen einen Film gesehen. »Und du?«, fragt Maria. Jonas schweigt. Sein Wochenende: Sofa. Er braucht eine bessere Geschichte.

activities.prompt: Give Jonas one opening sentence in German: First I had breakfast.
hints: The opening signpost first, then the perfect frame — the way Maria opened her story: Zuerst habe ich gefrühstückt.
activities.feedback: Zuerst habe ich gefrühstückt: Jonas can start with something true.

errors.explanation: With zuerst in first position the verb must follow: Zuerst habe ich gefrühstückt.

activities.body: Herr Meyer from 3B hasn't been seen for a week. His mailbox overflows. Lena stares at his door and guesses: »Er wird wohl krank sein.«
Evening: light in his window! »Er wird schon zu Hause sein«, whispers Lena. »Oder — er wird wohl Besuch haben.« She invents a cousin from Hamburg.
The door opens. Herr Meyer — with a suitcase and a tan. »Mallorca«, he says. »Zwei Wochen!« Lena laughs. Ihre Vermutung: falsch. Aber fast.

activities.prompt: Write Lena’s guess in German: He is probably tanned.
hints: The same guess frame as the sick guess, with braun before sein: Er wird wohl braun sein — the tan was the clue.
activities.feedback: Er wird wohl braun sein: the tan is the clue.

errors.explanation: ist stays in the present. The guess frame taught here uses wird + sein at the end: Er wird wohl braun sein.
The guess frame closes with the infinitive sein: Er wird wohl braun sein.

activities.body: January 1st. Three friends, three Vorsätze. Jonas: »Ich habe vor, mehr Sport zu machen.« Maria: »Mein Vorsatz: weniger Süßes.« Tim: »Ab Montag höre ich auf — mit dem Naschen!«
January 15th. Jonas runs twice a week — barely. Maria eats one chocolate bar instead of three. Tim? Tim nascht. Still. Every day.
February 1st. Jonas: »Ich werde mehr reisen — das ist leichter.« Maria smiles: »Mein Vorsatz bleibt.« Tim buys chocolate. »Ab Montag«, he says again.

activities.prompt: Write Tim’s new resolution in German: I intend to snack less.
hints: Tim's promise in the same frame, with the OPPOSITE amount word — less, not more: Ich habe vor, weniger zu naschen.
activities.feedback: Ich habe vor, weniger zu naschen: a clearer promise than “on Monday.”

answers: Ich habe vor, weniger zu naschen.

errors.explanation: The zu-infinitive completes the frame: Ich habe vor, weniger zu naschen.

errors.answer: Ich habe vor, mehr zu naschen.
errors.explanation: mehr would RAISE the snacking. Tim's resolution is to snack less: weniger zu naschen.

lessons.title: Mission: ein Kaffee in Berlin
lessons.objective: Walk into a Berlin café and order a coffee — your first real conversation in German.

lessons.title: Introducing yourself
lessons.objective: Introduce yourself with the verb heißen, and ask a question by moving the verb in front of the person.

legacyExercises.prompt: German has a verb that means 'to be called'. Which of these introduces you with that verb?
legacyExercises.explanation: Ich heiße Anna is literally 'I am called Anna'. Ich bin Anna also gives a name, but it uses plain 'to be', and Wie heißt du? is the question, not an introduction.

legacyExercises.prompt: You meet a neighbour and give your name with the verb that means 'to be called'.
legacyExercises.explanation: Ich heiße, not Ich bin, when the verb 'to be called' carries the name.

legacyExercises.prompt: The three words are out of order. Build the sentence in which Anna is called by name using heißen.
legacyExercises.explanation: Use heiße with ich and heißt with du. The verb sits second, and Ich keeps its capital as it opens the sentence.

legacyExercises.prompt: Your new colleague has introduced himself. Answer with the short German phrase for 'Nice to meet you'.
legacyExercises.explanation: Freut mich is the short reply German uses straight after an introduction.

legacyExercises.prompt: Learn a classmate's name by asking the question in which the verb comes before the person.
legacyExercises.explanation: German forms this question by putting heißt before du, with Wie in front — no extra helping word is needed.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the exchange. The first line puts the verb before the person to ask something. Whose name is being asked for?
legacyExercises.explanation: The opening Wie heißt du? asks the second speaker, Leo, for his name, and he answers with the same verb.
legacyExercises.passage:
— Wie heißt du?
— Ich heiße Leo. Und du?
— Ich heiße Anna.
— Freut mich, Anna.
legacyExercises.translation:
— What are you called?
— I am called Leo. And you?
— I am called Anna.
— Nice to meet you, Anna.

lessons.culturalNote: Wie heißt du? uses informal du for peers. German has a separate formal form with Sie; this lesson practices only the informal question.

lessons.title: At the café
lessons.objective: Order a drink and meet the article that changes shape once the drink is the object: einen.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which request uses the article German gives a masculine drink when it is the thing being ordered?
legacyExercises.explanation: Einen is the form a masculine noun takes as the object being ordered. Ein would leave the coffee standing as a bare subject.

legacyExercises.prompt: You are at the counter and coffee is what you want. Make the short request, keeping the article in its object form.
legacyExercises.explanation: Einen Kaffee, bitte — the object form einen survives even in the short request.

legacyExercises.prompt: The words are shuffled. Build the full polite request for one coffee.
legacyExercises.explanation: The verb möchte comes second and the object einen Kaffee follows it; bitte closes the request.

legacyExercises.prompt: Order a tea the same polite way, changing only the drink and keeping the object article.
legacyExercises.explanation: Same frame, different drink: einen Tee. The article stays einen because Tee is masculine too.

answers: I would like a coffee, please.
legacyExercises.prompt: Give the English meaning: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte.
legacyExercises.explanation: A request, not a statement about possession: möchte is 'would like'.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the café exchange. Which word marks the drink as the thing being ordered?
legacyExercises.explanation: Einen is the object form of the article; the coffee is what is being requested.
legacyExercises.passage:
— Guten Tag. Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte.
— Sofort. Und etwas dazu?
— Nein, danke.
legacyExercises.translation:
— Good day. I would like a coffee, please.
— Right away. And something with it?
— No, thank you.

lessons.culturalNote: A greeting before a request and thanks afterward make this small exchange courteous.

lessons.title: Numbers and quantities
lessons.objective: Count one to ten, then meet the point where German turns its numbers around: twenty-one is one-and-twenty.

legacyExercises.prompt: Start on the first run of five. Which German word is the number three?
legacyExercises.explanation: Drei is three, and it sits in the first run, eins to fünf. The second run, sechs to zehn, only begins after that.

legacyExercises.prompt: Put the German words in order to ask what one coffee costs.
legacyExercises.explanation: Was kostet goes first as a fixed pair, then the thing being priced. Ein Kaffee here is the label form of 'one coffee'.

legacyExercises.prompt: Say in German: Two apples, please.
legacyExercises.explanation: Äpfel is a noun, so it keeps its capital and takes a plural ending on top of it. The number itself stays zwei.

legacyExercises.prompt: Think: you want one coffee and no price is on the board. Ask the question in German, then write it.
legacyExercises.explanation: Was kostet asks the price of one thing, and you have just built this question. Say it aloud before you check.

lessons.culturalNote: A price question can be brief and direct; bitte still makes a request polite.

lessons.title: Story: lost in the old town
lessons.objective: Follow a lost tourist through the old town — and find the way.

lessons.title: Conversation: haggling at the flea market
lessons.objective: Ask prices, react to them, and close the deal — in German.

lessons.title: Days and times
lessons.objective: Meet the sun, the moon and the old gods hiding in the German week, and the one weekday that names nobody.

legacyExercises.prompt: A Berlin calendar marks each day with one word. Which is the word for today?
legacyExercises.explanation: Heute is the one. Morgen, Mittwoch and Woche name tomorrow, Wednesday and the week.

legacyExercises.prompt: Most German weekdays carry a sun, a moon or a god. Which one names nobody and simply marks the middle of the week?
legacyExercises.explanation: Mittwoch is literally mid-week. Donnerstag thunders with Donar and Sonntag belongs to the sun.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the week. Which day does the passage place in the middle?
legacyExercises.explanation: The fourth sentence says it outright: Mittwoch ist die Mitte der Woche.
legacyExercises.passage: Sonntag ist der Tag der Sonne. Am Montag arbeite ich. Am Dienstag lerne ich Deutsch. Mittwoch ist die Mitte der Woche. Am Donnerstag regnet es.
legacyExercises.translation: Sunday is the day of the sun. On Monday I work. On Tuesday I learn German. Wednesday is the middle of the week. On Thursday it rains.

legacyExercises.prompt: Build the German sentence for on Monday I work, with the day in first position.
legacyExercises.explanation: German likes the day in front: Am Montag, then the verb arbeite, then ich.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete with the noun for the morning, not the word for tomorrow: Der ___ ist kalt.
legacyExercises.explanation: Der Morgen, with the capital letter and the article, is the morning; morgen alone means tomorrow.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: today is Sunday.
legacyExercises.explanation: Heute ist plus the day. Sonntag is the sun's day, the name sitting in plain sight.

legacyExercises.prompt: Give the English meaning: Am Montag arbeite ich.
legacyExercises.explanation: German opens with the day and puts the verb straight after it: am Montag, then arbeite.

lessons.culturalNote: The week in Germany starts on Monday, so Montag is the first working day.

lessons.title: Home and articles
lessons.objective: Give every room and piece of furniture its der, die or das.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which one is the kitchen?
legacyExercises.explanation: Küche is feminine, so it takes die: die Küche. Tisch and Stuhl are masculine (der), Bett is neuter (das).

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the article before you write it: That is a chair.
legacyExercises.explanation: Stuhl is masculine, and masculine nouns take ein: Das ist ein Stuhl.

legacyExercises.prompt: Tisch is masculine. Pick the sentence that says that is a table.
legacyExercises.explanation: Masculine Tisch takes ein. Eine is only for feminine nouns, and einen is the accusative form — not needed after ist.

legacyExercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say that is a kitchen.
legacyExercises.explanation: Küche is feminine, so the article is eine: Das ist eine Küche.

legacyExercises.prompt: Make it about the bed: Das ist ein Stuhl.
legacyExercises.explanation: Bett is neuter, and neuter nouns take ein just like masculine ones: Das ist ein Bett.

legacyExercises.prompt: Zimmer is neuter. Fill in the article: Das ist ___ Zimmer.
legacyExercises.explanation: Zimmer is neuter, so the article is ein: Das ist ein Zimmer.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the note about a small apartment. Which room is new?
legacyExercises.explanation: The note calls the kitchen neu and everything else klein or alt: Die Küche ist neu.
legacyExercises.passage: Ich wohne in einer kleinen Wohnung. Das Zimmer ist klein und das Bett ist alt. Die Küche ist neu und der Tisch ist groß.
legacyExercises.translation: I live in a small apartment. The room is small and the bed is old. The kitchen is new and the table is big.

lessons.culturalNote: Germans learn every noun with its article — der, die or das — because the gender decides the shape of ein, mein and many other small words later.

lessons.title: Describing things
lessons.objective: Describe your home with adjectives that never change.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which one means ‘the house is big’?
legacyExercises.explanation: Groß is big, so das Haus ist groß is the house is big. Klein is small, neu is new, and the last option describes the room, not the house.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: The room is small.
legacyExercises.explanation: Zimmer is neuter but the adjective does not care: Das Zimmer ist klein.

legacyExercises.prompt: Pick the sentence that is correct German.
legacyExercises.explanation: After ist the adjective keeps its plain form — große is wrong — and sehr must stand before the adjective, not before ist.

legacyExercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say the kitchen is new.
legacyExercises.explanation: Die Küche ist neu: the adjective neu needs no ending after ist.

legacyExercises.prompt: Make it old instead of new: Das Auto ist neu.
legacyExercises.explanation: Swap neu for alt and nothing else moves: Das Auto ist alt.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete with the word for very: Das Haus ist ___ groß.
legacyExercises.explanation: Sehr sits directly before the adjective: Das Haus ist sehr groß.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the note. Which room is new and very big?
legacyExercises.explanation: Only the kitchen gets both neu and sehr groß: Die Küche ist neu und sehr groß.
legacyExercises.passage: Mein Haus ist alt, aber die Küche ist neu und sehr groß. Das Zimmer ist klein und sehr alt. Der Tisch ist groß.
legacyExercises.translation: My house is old, but the kitchen is new and very big. The room is small and very old. The table is big.

lessons.culturalNote: German homes are often described room by room — Küche, Zimmer, Bad — and neu versus alt is the first judgment every apartment viewing invites.

lessons.title: Build it: plurals
lessons.objective: Assemble plural sentences — die for every plural, verb agrees.

lessons.title: Work and daily routine
lessons.objective: Say what you do and when, with the time word behind the verb.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which one means ‘to work’?
legacyExercises.explanation: Arbeiten is to work. Lernen is to learn, wohnen is to live, lesen is to read.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: I learn in the evening.
legacyExercises.explanation: Lernen drops the -n for ich, and abends sits right after the verb: Ich lerne abends.

legacyExercises.prompt: Pick the sentence with the verb and the time word in the right places.
legacyExercises.explanation: The verb comes second and keeps its ich-form arbeite; morgens follows it. The other two break the verb or the order.

legacyExercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say I learn at midday.
legacyExercises.explanation: Ich lerne mittags: ich-form of the verb, then the when-word.

legacyExercises.prompt: Change the verb to work: Ich lerne abends.
legacyExercises.explanation: Swap lerne for arbeite and keep abends where it is: Ich arbeite abends.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete with the ich-form of arbeiten: Ich ___ morgens.
legacyExercises.explanation: Arbeiten becomes arbeite with ich: Ich arbeite morgens.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the day plan. When does the writer eat?
legacyExercises.explanation: The plan puts eating at midday: Mittags esse ich.
legacyExercises.passage: Ich arbeite morgens und lerne abends. Mittags esse ich. Nachts schlafe ich.
legacyExercises.translation: I work in the morning and learn in the evening. At midday I eat. At night I sleep.

lessons.culturalNote: Feierabend — the moment work ends for the day — is a beloved German word; the routine words in this lesson are the vocabulary it is built from.

lessons.objective: Assemble negations — kein for nouns, nicht for the rest.

lessons.title: Food and drink
lessons.objective: Say what you eat, drink and like.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which one is the cheese?
legacyExercises.explanation: Käse is masculine: der Käse. Brot and Wasser are neuter (das), Apfel is masculine too but it is the apple.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: I eat bread.
legacyExercises.explanation: Essen becomes esse for ich: Ich esse Brot.

legacyExercises.prompt: Pick the correct sentence.
legacyExercises.explanation: Trinken becomes trinke for ich. Trinkst belongs to du, and the infinitive cannot follow ich.

legacyExercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say I like cheese.
legacyExercises.explanation: Ich mag Käse: mögen takes the noun directly, no preposition needed.

legacyExercises.prompt: Change the verb to like: Ich esse Brot.
legacyExercises.explanation: Esse becomes mag, and Brot stays right where it is: Ich mag Brot.

legacyExercises.prompt: Apfel is masculine and the direct object. Fill in the article: Ich esse ___ Apfel.
legacyExercises.explanation: Masculine accusative: einen Apfel — the einen you met with einen Bruder.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the food diary. What does the writer drink in the morning?
legacyExercises.explanation: Morgens pairs Brot with Wasser: Ich trinke Wasser.
legacyExercises.passage: Ich esse morgens Brot und trinke Wasser. Mittags esse ich Käse. Ich mag Äpfel sehr.
legacyExercises.translation: In the morning I eat bread and drink water. At midday I eat cheese. I like apples very much.

lessons.culturalNote: Brot is a food group of its own in Germany — Abendbrot, the evening bread meal, is still dinner in many households.

lessons.title: Mine and yours
lessons.objective: Claim things with mein, dein, sein and ihr.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which one means ‘your’ (informal)?
legacyExercises.explanation: Dein is your. Mein is my, sein is his, ihr is her.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: That is my bag.
legacyExercises.explanation: Tasche is feminine, so mein becomes meine: Das ist meine Tasche.

legacyExercises.prompt: Tasche is feminine. Pick the correct sentence.
legacyExercises.explanation: Feminine nouns need the -e: meine Tasche. Meinen is accusative masculine — wrong noun, wrong case.

legacyExercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say that is his car.
legacyExercises.explanation: Auto is neuter, so sein stays bare: Das ist sein Auto.

legacyExercises.prompt: Make it her car: Das ist sein Auto.
legacyExercises.explanation: Sein becomes ihr; Auto is neuter so no ending appears: Das ist ihr Auto.

legacyExercises.prompt: Fill in the possessive for ‘your’: Das ist ___ Bruder.
legacyExercises.explanation: Your is dein, and Bruder is masculine so it stays bare: Das ist dein Bruder.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the introductions. Whose bag is small?
legacyExercises.explanation: Ihre Tasche points back to the sister: meine Schwester.
legacyExercises.passage: Das ist mein Bruder. Das ist meine Schwester. Sein Auto ist neu, aber ihre Tasche ist klein.
legacyExercises.translation: That is my brother. That is my sister. His car is new, but her bag is small.

lessons.culturalNote: Mein and dein mark the informal du-world; with strangers Germans switch to Ihr — the same word, capitalized, and a whole different distance.

lessons.title: Making plans
lessons.objective: Plan tomorrow and next week in the present tense.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which one means ‘next week’?
legacyExercises.explanation: Nächste Woche is next week. Letzte is last, diese is this, jede is every.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: Tomorrow I am working.
legacyExercises.explanation: Morgen first, verb second, subject after: Morgen arbeite ich.

answers: Nächste Woche fliege ich nach Berlin.
legacyExercises.prompt: Pick the correct sentence for ‘Next week I’m flying to Berlin’.
legacyExercises.explanation: The verb stays second even after a time phrase: Nächste Woche fliege ich nach Berlin.
options: Nächste Woche fliege ich nach Berlin.
Nächste Woche ich fliege nach Berlin.
Nächste Woche fliegen ich nach Berlin.

legacyExercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say tomorrow I’m learning.
legacyExercises.explanation: Morgen lerne ich: time first, verb second, subject third.

legacyExercises.prompt: Move the plan to next week: Morgen arbeite ich.
legacyExercises.explanation: Swap the time word; the verb keeps second place: Nächste Woche arbeite ich.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete with the word for ‘soon’: ___ besuche ich meine Eltern.
legacyExercises.explanation: Bald means soon and takes first position: Bald besuche ich meine Eltern.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the plan. When does the writer visit the parents?
legacyExercises.explanation: The parents get nächste Woche: nächste Woche besuche ich meine Eltern.
legacyExercises.passage: Mein Plan: morgen lerne ich. Nächste Woche besuche ich meine Eltern. Bald fliege ich nach Wien.
legacyExercises.translation: My plan: tomorrow I learn. Next week I visit my parents. Soon I fly to Vienna.

lessons.culturalNote: Germans plan ahead and say so — einen Plan haben is a virtue, and nächste Woche is the most-scheduled phrase in the language.

lessons.title: Months, seasons and dates
lessons.objective: Name the months and write a German date.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which one is ‘May’?
legacyExercises.explanation: Mai is May. März is March, Juni is June, Juli is July.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: My birthday is in May.
legacyExercises.explanation: In a month is im — in plus dem contracted: Mein Geburtstag ist im Mai.

legacyExercises.prompt: Pick the correct date.
legacyExercises.explanation: Dates take am, and the month never changes its form: am 3. Mai.

legacyExercises.prompt: Arrange the words to say winter is cold.
legacyExercises.explanation: Der Winter ist kalt: seasons are masculine, so der.

legacyExercises.prompt: Change the season: Der Sommer ist warm.
legacyExercises.explanation: Sommer becomes Winter and warm becomes kalt: Der Winter ist kalt.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete with the word for ‘in’ (a month): Mein Geburtstag ist ___ Mai.
legacyExercises.explanation: In plus dem contracts to im: Mein Geburtstag ist im Mai.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the note. When is the writer’s birthday?
legacyExercises.explanation: The date sits in the first sentence: Mein Geburtstag ist am 3. Mai.
legacyExercises.passage: Mein Geburtstag ist am 3. Mai. Im Sommer besuche ich meine Familie. Der Winter ist kalt, aber ich mag den Winter.
legacyExercises.translation: My birthday is on May 3rd. In summer I visit my family. Winter is cold, but I like winter.

lessons.culturalNote: Birthdays matter in Germany — colleagues expect cake from the birthday person, not the other way round, and the date always comes with its dot.

lessons.objective: Assemble Perfekt sentences tile by tile — haben second, participle last.

lessons.objective: Pull the sein-Perfekt back out of memory — movement takes sein.

lessons.objective: Tell a Saturday story with zuerst, dann, danach, am Ende.

lessons.objective: Assemble future sentences — werden second, infinitive last.

lessons.title: Würde: wishes and polite would
lessons.objective: Soften everything with würde + infinitive: Ich würde gern helfen.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
legacyExercises.explanation: Ich würde gern helfen — würde + gern + infinitive. Ich würde gern helfe breaks the infinitive, and ich werde is future, not 'would'.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict and write: I would like to travel.
legacyExercises.explanation: Ich würde gern reisen.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which form belongs to du?
legacyExercises.explanation: Du würdest — the -st ending. Würde is ich and er, würden is wir and sie.

legacyExercises.prompt: Arrange the words: would you help me?
legacyExercises.explanation: Würdest du mir helfen?

legacyExercises.prompt: Soften the command: Hilf mir!
legacyExercises.explanation: Würdest du mir helfen? — the polite upgrade.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete the wish: Ich ___ gern nach Italien reisen.
legacyExercises.explanation: Würde: Ich würde gern nach Italien reisen.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the wishes. Where would the speaker like to live?
legacyExercises.explanation: In Italien — Eigentlich würde ich gern in Italien leben.
legacyExercises.passage: Ich habe einen Wunsch: ich würde gern mehr reisen. Eigentlich würde ich gern in Italien leben. Würdest du mitkommen? Das wäre toll!
legacyExercises.translation: I have a wish: I would like to travel more. Actually I would like to live in Italy. Would you come along? That would be great!

lessons.culturalNote: Würde is the politeness engine of German — requests, wishes and hypotheticals all run on it. Master würde and you instantly sound friendlier.

lessons.title: Conversation: the hotel front desk
lessons.objective: Check in politely, ask for what you need, and handle the small problems — in German.

lessons.title: Remember: impossible wishes
lessons.objective: Pull wäre, hätte, könnte back out of memory — the grammar of daydreams.

lessons.title: Build it: relative clauses
lessons.objective: Assemble relative clauses — the pronoun copies the gender, the verb goes last.

lessons.title: Komparativ: bigger, better
lessons.objective: Compare with -er and als: größer als, besser als.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which means 'cheaper than'?
legacyExercises.explanation: Billiger als — -er plus als. Billiger wie breaks the als-rule.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict and write: Berlin is bigger than Munich.
legacyExercises.explanation: Berlin ist größer als München.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which is the comparative of gut?
legacyExercises.explanation: Besser — the rebel. Guter is just declined gut.

legacyExercises.prompt: Arrange the words: tea is healthier than coffee.
legacyExercises.explanation: Tee ist gesünder als Kaffee.

answers: Das Hotel ist teurer als das Hostel.
legacyExercises.prompt: Compare the two: Das Hotel ist teuer. Das Hostel ist billig.
legacyExercises.explanation: Das Hotel ist teurer als das Hostel.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete the comparison: Mein Auto ist schneller ___ dein Auto.
legacyExercises.explanation: Als — schneller als.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the comparison. What is cheaper than in town?
legacyExercises.explanation: Das Frühstück — breakfast is billiger als in der Stadt.
legacyExercises.passage: Zwei Hotels: Das Hotel Adlon ist teurer als das Hostel. Aber das Hostel ist besser als sein Ruf! Die Zimmer sind größer als im Hotel, und das Frühstück ist billiger als in der Stadt.
legacyExercises.translation: Two hotels: Hotel Adlon is more expensive than the hostel. But the hostel is better than its reputation! The rooms are bigger than in the hotel, and breakfast is cheaper than in town.

lessons.culturalNote: Als vs wie trips up even natives in speech — the rule is simple: -er always pairs with als. 'Größer als', never 'größer wie'.

lessons.title: Remember: the superlative
lessons.objective: Pull am besten and der schnellste back out of memory.

lessons.title: Wechselpräpositionen: wo vs wohin
lessons.objective: Choose Dativ for wo and Akkusativ for wohin: in der Küche vs in die Küche.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which sentence answers 'wohin?'?
legacyExercises.explanation: Ich gehe in die Küche — wohin takes Akkusativ. Ich bin in der Küche answers wo.

answers: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
Das Buch ist auf dem Tisch.
legacyExercises.prompt: Predict and write: The book is on the table. (wo?)
legacyExercises.explanation: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch — wo takes Dativ.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete the wo-sentence: Ich sitze auf ___ Stuhl.
legacyExercises.explanation: Dem — auf + Dativ masculine: auf dem Stuhl.

answers: Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch.
legacyExercises.prompt: Arrange the words: I'm putting the book on the table.
legacyExercises.explanation: Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch — wohin takes Akkusativ.

answers: Ich hänge das Bild an die Wand.
legacyExercises.prompt: Answer 'wohin': Das Bild hängt an der Wand.
legacyExercises.explanation: Ich hänge das Bild an die Wand.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete the direction: Wir gehen in ___ Park.
legacyExercises.explanation: Den — wohin takes Akkusativ: in den Park.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the move. Where does the picture hang?
legacyExercises.explanation: Über dem Sofa — above the sofa.
legacyExercises.passage: Wir stellen das Sofa an die Wand. Der Stuhl steht neben dem Tisch. Das Bild hängt über dem Sofa. Die Lampe liegt noch auf dem Boden — wir stellen sie in die Ecke.
legacyExercises.translation: We're putting the sofa against the wall. The chair stands next to the table. The picture hangs above the sofa. The lamp is still lying on the floor — we're putting it in the corner.

lessons.culturalNote: 'Wo?' or 'wohin?' — Germans ask it instinctively. Get this right and your directions stop sounding lost.

lessons.title: Passiv mit werden
lessons.objective: Describe processes passively: Das Auto wird repariert.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which sentence is passive?
legacyExercises.explanation: Die Briefe werden geschrieben — werden + participle. Werden schreiben is future; schreibt er is active.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict and write: The car is being repaired.
legacyExercises.explanation: Das Auto wird repariert.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete the passive: Das Haus ___ gebaut.
legacyExercises.explanation: Wird — singular: Das Haus wird gebaut. Wurde is past.

legacyExercises.prompt: Arrange the words: German is spoken here.
legacyExercises.explanation: Hier wird Deutsch gesprochen.

legacyExercises.prompt: Rewrite in the passive: Man repariert das Auto.
legacyExercises.explanation: Das Auto wird repariert.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete the notice: Die Pakete werden morgen ___.
legacyExercises.explanation: Geliefert: Die Pakete werden morgen geliefert.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the factory tour. What happens to the products here?
legacyExercises.explanation: Sie werden gebaut und verkauft — built and sold here.
legacyExercises.passage: In der Fabrik wird viel gearbeitet. Die Produkte werden hier gebaut und dann verkauft. Jeden Tag werden tausend Pakete geliefert. Hier wird Deutsch gesprochen.
legacyExercises.translation: A lot is worked in the factory. The products are built here and then sold. Every day a thousand parcels are delivered. German is spoken here.

lessons.culturalNote: German news and manuals live in the passive — 'Hier wird Deutsch gesprochen' is on signs everywhere. It sounds official without naming anyone.

lessons.title: Berufe und Bewerbung
lessons.objective: Talk about jobs and applications: der Beruf, die Stelle, das Vorstellungsgespräch.

legacyExercises.prompt: Which means 'the job interview'?
legacyExercises.explanation: Das Vorstellungsgespräch. Die Stelle is the position, der Beruf the profession.

legacyExercises.prompt: Predict and write: The interview is on Monday.
legacyExercises.explanation: Das Vorstellungsgespräch ist am Montag.

answers: Ich bewerbe mich um eine Stelle.
legacyExercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
legacyExercises.explanation: Ich bewerbe mich um eine Stelle — bewerben needs mich + um. The others drop or scramble the mich.
options: Ich bewerbe mich um eine Stelle.
Ich bewerbe mir um eine Stelle.
Ich mich bewerbe um eine Stelle.

answers: Ich bewerbe mich um eine Stelle.
legacyExercises.prompt: Arrange the words: I am applying for a position.
legacyExercises.explanation: Ich bewerbe mich um eine Stelle.

answers: Ich bewerbe mich um die Stelle.
legacyExercises.prompt: Say it with bewerben: Ich will die Stelle.
legacyExercises.explanation: Ich bewerbe mich um die Stelle.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete the application: Ich bewerbe mich ___ eine Stelle als Lehrer.
legacyExercises.explanation: Um: Ich bewerbe mich um eine Stelle als Lehrer.

legacyExercises.prompt: Read the job ad. What should you send?
legacyExercises.explanation: Ihren Lebenslauf — your CV.
legacyExercises.passage: Stellenanzeige: Wir suchen einen Mitarbeiter. Der Beruf: Verkäufer. Das Gehalt ist gut. Bitte schicken Sie Ihren Lebenslauf. Das Vorstellungsgespräch ist nächste Woche.
legacyExercises.translation: Job ad: We're looking for an employee. The profession: salesperson. The salary is good. Please send your CV. The interview is next week.

lessons.culturalNote: The Bewerbung is a ritual — Lebenslauf, Anschreiben, Vorstellungsgespräch. Germans take the paperwork as seriously as the interview.

lessons.title: Mission: Das Bewerbungsgespräch
lessons.objective: Survive a German job interview: introduce yourself, describe experience, stay polite.
